questions.s: Concerning the general plan of the brain (Last's):
o: The diencephalon's main parts are the thalamus and hypothalamus

The diencephalon consists mainly of the thalamus and hypothalamus (with the epithalamus and subthalamus), and its cavity is the third ventricle.
The cerebral hemispheres (telencephalon) surround it. (Last's p. 577)
The hindbrain consists of the pons and medulla only

Last's says the hindbrain consists of the pons, the medulla oblongata and the cerebellum.
The cerebellum is part of the hindbrain, developing from the rhombic lips of the metencephalon. (Last's p. 577)
The medulla becomes the spinal cord where the first cervical nerve roots emerge

The medulla changes its name to spinal cord at the uppermost rootlets of the first cervical nerve, just below the foramen magnum.
The pyramidal decussation lies at about this level. (Last's p. 577)
CSF leaves the ventricles through foramina in the roof of the third ventricle

CSF can only leave the ventricular system through foramina in the roof of the fourth ventricle (median and lateral apertures), in the medulla. The third ventricle has no such openings.
That is why blockage of the aqueduct or fourth ventricle outlets causes obstructive hydrocephalus. (Last's p. 577)

questions.s: The surfaces of the cerebral hemisphere:
o: The orbital surface of the frontal lobe is slightly concave

The orbital surface of the frontal lobe is slightly concave, from the impression of the orbital plates in the anterior cranial fossa.
Its gyri are named orbital gyri and the gyrus rectus. (Last's p. 577)
The temporal pole is concave in conformity with the middle cranial fossa

Last's says the temporal pole is boldly convex, fitting the deep concavity of the middle cranial fossa.
"Concave" is the changed word; the fossa is concave, the pole convex. (Last's p. 577)
The under surface of the occipital lobe slopes downwards and outwards

The under surface of the occipital lobe slopes downward and outward, conforming with the tentorium cerebelli on which it rests.
That is why it is called the tentorial surface. (Last's p. 577)
The under surface is more regular than the medial surface

Last's says the under surface of the hemisphere is more irregular than the medial surface.
The base has the orbital surface, temporal pole and tentorial surface at different levels. (Last's p. 577)

questions.s: Regarding the lobes of the cerebral hemisphere:
o: They are named after the cranial bones that lie adjacent

The frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes are named after the cranial bones that lie adjacent to them.
The lobes do not correspond exactly to the bones' borders. (Last's p. 577)
The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus

The parietal lobe is bounded in front by the central sulcus and below by the lateral sulcus.
Behind, it meets the occipital lobe at the parieto-occipital sulcus medially. (Last's p. 577)
The occipital lobe lies above and behind the parieto-occipital sulcus

The occipital lobe lies below and behind the parieto-occipital sulcus, not above it.
Medially, the parieto-occipital sulcus separates the precuneus (parietal, above) from the cuneus (occipital, below). (Last's p. 577)
The dominant hemisphere is usually slightly smaller than the other

One hemisphere, usually the left in right-handed people, is slightly larger and is the dominant hemisphere.
"Smaller" is the changed word. (Last's p. 577)
The part on the lateral surface is strictly the posterior ramus

The lateral sulcus begins on the inferior surface of the brain. The part seen on the lateral surface is strictly its posterior ramus.
The short anterior and ascending rami branch off near its front. (Last's p. 577-9)
The anterior and ascending rami penetrate the inferior frontal gyrus

The anterior and ascending rami of the lateral sulcus penetrate the inferior frontal gyrus, dividing it into orbital, triangular and opercular parts.
In the dominant hemisphere the triangular and opercular parts form Broca's area. (Last's p. 577-9)
The insula is almost completely surrounded by the cingulate sulcus

The insula is almost completely surrounded by the circular sulcus.
The cingulate sulcus lies on the medial surface above the cingulate gyrus. (Last's p. 577-9)
The opercula are formed by frontal, parietal and occipital cortex

The opercula covering the insula are formed by frontal, parietal and temporal cortex.
The occipital lobe does not reach the insula. (Last's p. 577-9)
Indents the superior border just behind the midpoint

The central sulcus indents the superior border of the hemisphere just behind its midpoint, then runs down and forward on the lateral surface.
It separates the precentral (motor) and postcentral (sensory) gyri. (Last's p. 577-9)
Is the only long sulcus to pass on to the medial surface

The central sulcus is the only long sulcus to pass on to the medial surface, where it is enclosed by the paracentral lobule.
This helps to identify it at operation and on imaging. (Last's p. 577-9)
Usually runs directly into the lateral sulcus

The central sulcus does not usually run into the lateral sulcus, which is a useful identifying point. A small bridge of cortex separates them.
The postcentral sulcus may join the lateral sulcus. (Last's p. 577-9)
Is enclosed on the medial surface by the cuneus

On the medial surface the central sulcus is enclosed by the paracentral lobule.
The cuneus is the wedge of occipital cortex between the parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci. (Last's p. 577-9)

questions.s: Regarding the parietal and occipital lobes on the lateral surface:
o: The supramarginal gyrus closes the posterior end of the lateral sulcus

The supramarginal gyrus arches around the upturned posterior end of the lateral sulcus.
The angular gyrus caps the end of the superior temporal sulcus. Both are in the inferior parietal lobule. (Last's p. 577-9)
The supramarginal gyrus closes the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus

The angular gyrus, not the supramarginal, closes the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus.
"Supramarginal: lateral sulcus; angular: superior temporal sulcus." (Last's p. 577-9)
The preoccipital notch is indented by a fold of dura over the transverse sinus

The slight preoccipital notch on the inferior border is made by a fold of dura over the transverse sinus. It marks the front of the occipital lobe on the lateral surface.
A line from it to the parieto-occipital sulcus demarcates the occipital lobe laterally. (Last's p. 577-9)
The occipital demarcation line slopes downwards at 90 degrees from the parieto-occipital sulcus

The demarcation line from the parieto-occipital sulcus slopes down at about 45 degrees to the preoccipital notch, not at 90 degrees.
There is no visible sulcus on the lateral surface; the boundary is arbitrary. (Last's p. 577-9)

questions.s: The medial surface of the hemisphere:
o: The cingulate gyrus lies above the corpus callosum

The cingulate gyrus lies above the corpus callosum, with the cingulate sulcus above it.
It is part of the limbic lobe. (Last's p. 579-81)
The precuneus lies between the parieto-occipital sulcus and the paracentral lobule

The precuneus is the medial parietal area between the parieto-occipital sulcus behind and the paracentral lobule in front.
It lies above the cuneus. (Last's p. 579-81)
The cuneus is limited superiorly by the calcarine sulcus

The cuneus is limited inferiorly by the calcarine sulcus, and above by the parieto-occipital sulcus.
So the cuneus is the upper bank of the visual cortex, representing the lower visual field. (Last's p. 579-81)
The parieto-occipital sulcus is horizontal

The parieto-occipital sulcus is oblique, running down and forward from the superior border to join the calcarine sulcus.
Together they form a Y on its side. (Last's p. 579-81)

questions.s: The calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci form a Y on its side; regarding this:
o: The common stem is the anterior part of the calcarine sulcus

The parieto-occipital sulcus joins the calcarine sulcus, so the part of the calcarine in front of the junction is the common stem of the Y.
This anterior part of the calcarine is not lined by visual cortex. (Last's p. 579-81)
The two limbs are the parieto-occipital sulcus and the posterior part of the calcarine sulcus

The two limbs of the Y are the parieto-occipital sulcus above and the posterior part of the calcarine sulcus below. Together they enclose the cuneus.
The visual cortex (area 17) lines the posterior calcarine sulcus. (Last's p. 579-81)
The lingual gyrus lies above the posterior part of the calcarine sulcus

The lingual gyrus lies below the posterior part of the calcarine sulcus. The cuneus lies above.
Lingual gyrus = lower bank = upper visual field. (Last's p. 579-81)
The lingual gyrus is limited inferiorly by the occipitotemporal sulcus

The lingual gyrus is limited inferiorly by the collateral sulcus.
The occipitotemporal sulcus lies further laterally on the tentorial surface. (Last's p. 579-81)

questions.s: The inferior surface of the brain:
o: The olfactory bulb lies on the gyrus rectus

The olfactory bulb lies on the gyrus rectus along the medial margin of the orbital surface, and the olfactory tract lies in the olfactory sulcus beside it.
The bulb rests on the cribriform plate. (Last's p. 581)
The olfactory tract runs in the collateral sulcus

The olfactory tract runs in the olfactory sulcus, alongside the gyrus rectus.
The collateral sulcus is on the tentorial (inferior temporal and occipital) surface. (Last's p. 581)
The occipitotemporal sulcus lies lateral to the collateral sulcus

On the tentorial surface two long sulci run from front to back: the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally and the collateral sulcus medially.
Between them lies the medial occipitotemporal gyrus. (Last's p. 581)
The parahippocampal gyrus lies lateral to the collateral sulcus

The parahippocampal gyrus lies medial to the collateral sulcus.
Its anterior end hooks back as the uncus. (Last's p. 581)

questions.s: Midline structures on the base of the brain:
o: The tuber cinereum lies behind the optic chiasma

The tuber cinereum lies behind the optic chiasma, and the pituitary stalk (infundibulum) projects down from it.
It forms part of the floor of the third ventricle. (Last's p. 581)
The mamillary bodies lie in front of the tuber cinereum

The mammillary bodies lie behind the tuber cinereum.
From front to back in the midline: optic chiasma, tuber cinereum with the stalk, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance. (Last's p. 581)
The posterior perforated substance lies deep in the angle between the cerebral peduncles

The posterior perforated substance lies deep in the angle between the cerebral peduncles, behind the mammillary bodies.
It is pierced by central branches of the posterior cerebral arteries. (Last's p. 581)
The anterior perforated substance lies on the temporal lobe medial to the uncus

The anterior perforated substance lies on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe immediately lateral to the optic chiasma, where the olfactory tract divides.
It is pierced by the lenticulostriate arteries. (Last's p. 581)
The thalamus is the largest mass of cells in each hemisphere

The thalamus is the largest mass of grey matter in each hemisphere, but it belongs to the diencephalon.
It is often grouped with the basal nuclei for convenience. (Last's p. 581)
The corpus striatum is the caudate nucleus and putamen

Last's defines the corpus striatum as the caudate nucleus and putamen, joined by interconnecting fibres (giving the striated look).
Note other texts call caudate plus putamen the striatum and include the globus pallidus in the corpus striatum. (Last's p. 581)
The globus pallidus is the outer part of the lentiform nucleus

The putamen is the outer (lateral) part of the lentiform nucleus. The globus pallidus is the inner (medial) part.
The external capsule lies lateral to the putamen. (Last's p. 581)
The main efferent pathway of the corpus striatum arises from the caudate nucleus

The main efferent pathway of the corpus striatum arises from the globus pallidus.
The caudate and putamen receive input; the pallidum sends output. (Last's p. 581)
The tail of the caudate joins the amygdaloid body

The comma-shaped caudate nucleus curves back from its head, around into the temporal lobe, and its tail ends in the amygdaloid body.
It follows the C-shaped curve of the lateral ventricle. (Last's p. 581-2)
The whole length of the caudate convexity projects into the lateral ventricle

The caudate nucleus bulges into the lateral ventricle along its whole length.
Head in the lateral wall of the anterior horn, body in the floor of the body, tail in the roof of the inferior horn. (Last's p. 581-2)
The putamen is small and conical; the globus pallidus large and quadrilateral

The putamen is large and roughly quadrilateral; the globus pallidus is small and bluntly conical.
The two together make the lens-shaped lentiform nucleus. (Last's p. 581-2)
The putamen joins the caudate head across the posterior limb of the internal capsule

The putamen joins the head of the caudate through bands of grey matter crossing the anterior limb of the internal capsule, giving the striated appearance.
The posterior limb has no such bridges. (Last's p. 581-2)
The amygdala lies in the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle

The amygdala lies in the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, at its tip, connected with the end of the caudate tail.
It lies deep to the uncus. (Last's p. 581-2)
The amygdala lies in the floor of the inferior horn

The amygdala lies in the roof of the inferior horn. The hippocampus forms the floor.
The amygdala is anterior and above; the hippocampus is behind and below. (Last's p. 581-2)
The claustrum lies lateral to the putamen

The claustrum is a thin sheet of grey matter lying lateral to the putamen, separated from it by the external capsule.
Last's says its significance is unknown. (Last's p. 581-2)
The claustrum lies between the putamen and globus pallidus

The claustrum lies lateral to the putamen, between the external and extreme capsules, not between the putamen and globus pallidus.
The putamen and pallidum are separated by the lateral medullary lamina. (Last's p. 581-2)
The striatum is the input side, receiving mainly from cortex, thalamus and substantia nigra

The striatum (caudate and putamen) is the input side of the basal nuclei, receiving mainly from the cortex, thalamus and substantia nigra.
Almost the whole cortex projects to it. (Last's p. 582)
The globus pallidus is the output side

The globus pallidus is the output side, projecting to the thalamus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra and reticular formation.
The thalamus then projects to the motor and premotor cortex. (Last's p. 582)
The ansa lenticularis passes dorsal to the subthalamic nucleus

Last's says the ansa lenticularis passes ventral to the subthalamic nucleus, and the ansa fascicularis (lenticular fasciculus) passes dorsal.
The ansa lenticularis loops around the edge of the capsule. (Last's p. 582)
The ansa lenticularis passes through the fibres of the internal capsule

It is the ansa fascicularis (and subthalamic fasciculus) that pass through the internal capsule. The ansa lenticularis loops around its medial edge.
"Ansa" means loop. (Last's p. 582)

questions.s: Parkinsonism and the cerebral white matter:
o: Parkinsonism shows a decrease of dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway

Parkinsonism shows a decrease of dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway, with tremor, rigidity and akinesia.
The pigmented neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta are lost. (Last's p. 583)
Association fibres are confined to their own hemisphere

Association (arcuate) fibres link areas of cortex within one hemisphere. Commissural fibres cross to the other side; projection fibres run to and from lower centres.
Short association fibres link adjacent gyri; long ones form named bundles (arcuate, uncinate, cingulum). (Last's p. 583)
Most commissural fibres are in the anterior commissure

Most commissural fibres are in the corpus callosum.
The anterior commissure is small, linking olfactory and temporal regions. (Last's p. 583)
Fibres of the corpus callosum run parallel to the corona radiata without crossing it

The fibres of the corpus callosum intersect the corona radiata as they pass laterally.
The two fibre systems cross each other in the centrum semiovale. (Last's p. 583)
It lies within the concavity of the C-shaped caudate nucleus

The internal capsule lies within the concavity of the C-shaped caudate nucleus, which separates it from the lateral ventricle.
The capsule is the lateral boundary of the caudate and thalamus. (Last's p. 583)
In horizontal section it is bent into a lateral concavity by the globus pallidus

In horizontal section the convex medial border of the lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus) bends the capsule into an L-shape, with anterior limb, genu and posterior limb.
The angle points medially at the genu. (Last's p. 583)
The anterior limb lies between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus

The anterior limb lies between the head of the caudate and the lentiform nucleus. The posterior limb lies between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus.
The genu is at the junction. (Last's p. 583)
Frontopontine fibres occupy the lateral third of the base of the peduncle

Frontopontine fibres occupy the medial third of the base of the cerebral peduncle.
The corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres occupy the middle three-fifths, and parieto-temporo-occipitopontine fibres the lateral part. (Last's p. 583)

questions.s: Regarding the components of the internal capsule:
o: The genu lies at the apex of the globus pallidus

The genu of the internal capsule lies at the apex (medial point) of the globus pallidus, at the bend of the L.
It sits close to the interventricular foramen. (Last's p. 583)
The genu carries corticonuclear fibres

The genu carries corticonuclear fibres to the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves.
Behind it, in the posterior limb, are the corticospinal fibres. (Last's p. 583)
Corticospinal fibres occupy the posterior two-thirds of the posterior limb

Last's says the corticospinal fibres occupy the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb. The posterior third carries sensory (thalamocortical) fibres.
So a lesion of the back of the posterior limb causes hemianaesthesia with less weakness. (Last's p. 583)
The anterior limb is thought to carry fibres from the frontal eye field to the abducent nucleus for accommodation

The anterior limb is thought to carry fibres from the frontal eye field to the oculomotor nucleus, for the accommodation–convergence reflex.
The abducent nucleus is not involved in accommodation. (Last's p. 583)

questions.s: In the posterior limb of the internal capsule (Last's):
o: Corticospinal fibres run arm, hand, trunk, leg and perineum from front to back

Behind the corticonuclear fibres in the genu, the corticospinal fibres in the posterior limb are arranged arm, hand, trunk, leg and perineum from front to back.
So the body is laid out in sequence from head (genu) to perineum (back). (Last's p. 583-4)
Corticospinal fibres run leg, trunk, arm in order from front to back

The order from front to back is arm, hand, trunk, leg, then perineum. Leg fibres are posterior, not anterior.
A memory aid: the face at the genu, then work down the body going backward. (Last's p. 583-4)
In the cerebral peduncle head fibres lie medially and perineal fibres laterally

In the base of the cerebral peduncle the same sequence runs from medial (head) to lateral (perineum).
The corticospinal fibres occupy the middle three-fifths of the base. (Last's p. 583-4)
Striate artery haemorrhage here typically causes ipsilateral flaccid paralysis

Haemorrhage from a striate (lenticulostriate) artery in the posterior limb causes contralateral paralysis, initially flaccid, becoming spastic: an upper motor neurone lesion.
The fibres have not yet crossed, so the paralysis is on the opposite side. (Last's p. 583-4)

questions.s: Fibre numbers in the internal capsule and corpus callosum:
o: Corticopontine fibres are the largest group in the internal capsule

Last's says corticopontine fibres are the largest group in the internal capsule, about 20 million.
They connect the cortex to the pontine nuclei and so to the cerebellum. (Last's p. 585)
Corticospinal fibres are the largest group in the internal capsule

Corticospinal fibres are fewer (about one million on each side). Corticopontine fibres are the largest group.
The corticopontocerebellar system is enormous, reflecting the cerebellum's role in planning movement. (Last's p. 585)
The corpus callosum has about 100 million fibres

The corpus callosum has about 100 million fibres, linking symmetrical parts of the two hemispheres.
It is by far the largest commissure. (Last's p. 585)
The corpus callosum becomes thinner from front to back

The corpus callosum becomes increasingly thicker from front to back, ending as the thick splenium.
The splenium is the thickest part. (Last's p. 585)
Commences at the anterior commissure at the upper end of the lamina terminalis

The corpus callosum begins at the anterior commissure at the upper end of the lamina terminalis, passing up as the rostrum.
The rostrum is thin and joins the lamina terminalis. (Last's p. 585)
The rostrum passes upwards and forwards from the anterior commissure

From the anterior commissure the rostrum passes upward and forward, then turns back as the genu.
The body then runs backward to the splenium. (Last's p. 585)
Has three parts: genu, body and splenium

Last's describes four parts: rostrum, genu, body and splenium.
The rostrum is easily forgotten; it is the thin part continuous with the lamina terminalis. (Last's p. 585)
Ends posteriorly as a thin tapering edge

Posteriorly the corpus callosum ends as a thick, rounded free border, the splenium.
The great cerebral vein lies just below the splenium. (Last's p. 585)
Genu fibres form the forceps minor

Fibres from the genu arch forward to the frontal lobes as the forceps minor.
They form a U-shape seen on horizontal sections. (Last's p. 586)
Splenial fibres form the forceps minor

Fibres from the splenium form the forceps major, passing back to the occipital lobes.
Minor = genu = frontal; major = splenium = occipital. (Last's p. 586)
Fibres form the roof of the anterior horn and body of the lateral ventricle

Callosal fibres sweeping laterally form the roof of the anterior horn and body of the lateral ventricle.
In the temporal lobe they form the tapetum. (Last's p. 586)
The tapetum forms the medial wall of the inferior and posterior horns

The tapetum forms the lateral wall (and roof) of the inferior and posterior horns, not the medial wall.
The medial wall of the posterior horn has the calcar avis and bulb of the posterior horn. (Last's p. 586)
MsI includes Brodmann areas 4 and 6

Last's uses MsI for the primary motor region, including Brodmann areas 4 and 6 (the old motor and premotor regions).
"Ms" means mainly motor, with some sensory function. (Last's p. 586)
MsII is the supplementary motor area on the medial frontal surface

MsII is the supplementary motor area on the medial surface of the frontal lobe, parts of areas 6 and 8.
It is concerned with planning and posture. (Last's p. 586)
SmI corresponds to areas 40 and 43

SmI corresponds to areas 3, 1 and 2 (the postcentral gyrus). Areas 40 and 43 form SmII.
"Sm" means mainly sensory. (Last's p. 586)
SmII is the uppermost part of the postcentral gyrus

SmII is the lowest part of the postcentral gyrus (and adjacent parietal operculum), not the uppermost part.
Last's associates it with pain and temperature. (Last's p. 586)
MsI receives its main inputs from the cerebellum and thalamus

MsI (primary motor cortex) receives its main input from the cerebellum, relayed through the thalamus.
This links cerebellar coordination to voluntary movement. (Last's p. 586)
MsII receives many fibres from the basal nuclei

MsII receives many fibres from the basal nuclei and is concerned with postural mechanisms.
So the cerebellum feeds mainly MsI and the basal nuclei mainly MsII. (Last's p. 586)
In the precentral gyrus the face is represented upside down

In the precentral gyrus the body is represented upside down, but the face itself is the right way up.
The leg is at the top (on the medial surface) and the face at the bottom. (Last's p. 586)
The hand area lies below the face area

The face lies lowest on the precentral gyrus, with the hand above it.
From below up: face, hand, arm, trunk, leg (on the medial surface). (Last's p. 586)
Broca's area is areas 44 and 45

Broca's motor speech area is areas 44 and 45 in the inferior frontal gyrus, usually on the left.
Area 44 is the pars opercularis and 45 the pars triangularis. (Last's p. 586)
Broca's area is centred on the pars triangularis

Broca's area is centred on the pars triangularis, between the anterior and ascending rami of the lateral sulcus.
It lies just in front of the face area of the motor cortex. (Last's p. 586)
Damage to Broca's area paralyses the laryngeal muscles

Damage to Broca's area causes motor (expressive) aphasia but does not paralyse the laryngeal muscles.
Speech muscles are bilaterally represented in the motor cortex, so unilateral lesions do not paralyse them. (Last's p. 586)
Wernicke's area lies in the anterior parts of the superior and middle temporal gyri

Wernicke's area lies in the posterior parts of the superior and middle temporal gyri, extending into the lower parietal lobe.
Damage causes receptive (fluent) aphasia with poor comprehension. (Last's p. 586)
The frontal eye field is in the centre of the middle frontal gyrus

The frontal eye field lies in the centre (posterior part) of the middle frontal gyrus, parts of areas 6, 8 and 9.
It drives conjugate eye movements to the opposite side. (Last's p. 586)
SmI is associated with pain and temperature

Last's associates SmI with touch, kinaesthetic and vibration sense. SmII appears to be associated with pain and temperature.
So primary sensory cortex is mainly discriminative. (Last's p. 586)
The cortex is necessary for localisation of pain

The cortex is necessary for localising pain, though conscious appreciation of pain may occur at thalamic level.
That is why thalamic lesions can cause severe, poorly localised pain. (Last's p. 586)
The gustatory area is in the superior part of the postcentral gyrus

The gustatory area is in the inferior part of the postcentral gyrus (frontoparietal operculum), near the tongue area, extending onto the insula.
The superior part represents the leg. (Last's p. 586)
The auditory area is areas 41 and 42

The primary auditory area is areas 41 and 42, in the anterior transverse temporal gyrus (Heschl's).
It lies within the lateral sulcus on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus. (Last's p. 586)
The auditory association area is area 21

The auditory association area is area 22, in the superior temporal gyrus.
Area 21 is the middle temporal gyrus. (Last's p. 586)
A lesion of one auditory cortex does not cause deafness

A lesion of one auditory cortex does not cause deafness, because each cochlea is represented bilaterally.
It may impair sound localisation in the opposite half of space. (Last's p. 586)
The olfactory area is in the posterior part of the parahippocampal gyrus

The olfactory area lies in the uncus, at the front of the parahippocampal gyrus, not its posterior part.
The posterior parahippocampal gyrus is involved in memory and visuospatial processing. (Last's p. 586)
It lies along the lower lip of the anterior part of the calcarine sulcus

The visual area (area 17) lies along the lower lip of the anterior part of the calcarine sulcus and both lips of its posterior part.
In front of the junction with the parieto-occipital sulcus, only the lower lip is visual cortex. (Last's p. 586-7)
It lies along the upper lip of the anterior part of the calcarine sulcus

In the anterior part of the calcarine sulcus the visual cortex lies on the lower lip, not the upper lip.
Both lips of the posterior part are visual cortex. (Last's p. 586-7)
It extends about 1 cm on to the lateral surface as far as the lunate sulcus

Area 17 extends about 1 cm onto the lateral surface of the occipital pole, as far as the lunate sulcus.
Macular vision is represented in this posterior part. (Last's p. 586-7)
The visual association areas are 17 and 18

The visual association areas are 18 and 19. Area 17 is the striate (primary) visual cortex.
Damage to 18 and 19 causes visual agnosia rather than blindness. (Last's p. 586-7)
The stria of Gennari bisects the grey matter of the striate cortex

The stria of Gennari, a band of myelinated fibres in layer 4, bisects the grey matter of the striate cortex and is visible to the naked eye.
It gives area 17 its name ("striate"). (Last's p. 586-7)
The upper half of each visual cortex receives from the upper half of each half-retina

The upper half of each visual cortex receives from the upper half of each half-retina. Since the upper retina sees the lower visual field, the visual fields are crossed vertically as well as horizontally.
So the cuneus (upper bank) represents the lower field. (Last's p. 586-7)
The macula registers at the anterior end of the visual area

The macula registers at the posterior end of the visual area, near the occipital pole.
Peripheral retina is represented further anteriorly. (Last's p. 586-7)
The temporal half of the retina receives from the temporal half of the visual field

The temporal half of each retina receives light from the nasal half of the visual field.
The optics of the eye invert the image: nasal field to temporal retina, upper field to lower retina. (Last's p. 586-7)
The bipolar cells represent the posterior root ganglion cells of other pathways

The bipolar cells of the retina are the first neurons of the visual pathway, equivalent to the posterior root ganglion cells of other sensory pathways.
The rods and cones are receptors. (Last's p. 587)
Ganglion cells are about 1 per cone and 1 per 80 rods

Cones have almost one ganglion cell each, giving high acuity, while about 80 rods converge on one ganglion cell, giving sensitivity in dim light.
This explains why central (cone) vision is sharp and peripheral (rod) vision is sensitive. (Last's p. 587)
Ganglion cells lie in the outer part of the retina next to the choroid

The ganglion cells lie in the inner part of the retina next to the vitreous. The rods and cones lie in the outer part next to the choroid.
So light passes through the whole retina before reaching the receptors. (Last's p. 587)
The optic nerve regenerates effectively after division

The optic nerve is CNS white matter, with oligodendrocytes, and shows no effective regeneration after division.
Peripheral nerves, with Schwann cells, can regenerate. (Last's p. 587)
The dura and arachnoid leave the nerve at the optic foramen

At the optic foramen the dura and arachnoid leave the nerve (the dura blending with periosteum), and the nerve continues intracranially sheathed in pia.
Within the orbit all three meninges ensheath the nerve. (Last's p. 587)
The chiasma is attached to the anterior part of the floor of the third ventricle

The optic chiasma is attached to the anterior part of the floor of the third ventricle, in front of the tuber cinereum.
The optic recess of the third ventricle lies above it. (Last's p. 587)
The right optic tract carries the temporal field of the right eye

The right optic tract carries fibres representing the left visual field: the nasal field of the right eye (from the right temporal retina) and the temporal field of the left eye (from the left nasal retina).
So it does not carry the right eye's temporal field. (Last's p. 587)
There is a further decussation of visual fibres between the optic tract and the cortex

There is no further decussation of visual fibres between the optic tract and the cortex.
The only crossing is at the chiasma. (Last's p. 587)

questions.s: The optic tract divides into two branches; regarding these:
o: The larger enters the lateral geniculate body

The larger, lateral branch of the optic tract enters the lateral geniculate body, where visual fibres synapse.
This is the pathway for conscious vision. (Last's p. 587)
The superior brachium is the larger branch

The superior brachium is the smaller, medial branch.
Most fibres go to the lateral geniculate body. (Last's p. 587)
The superior brachium passes between the lateral and medial geniculate bodies

The superior brachium passes between the lateral and medial geniculate bodies to reach the superior colliculus and pretectal nuclei.
It carries fibres for reflexes, not conscious vision. (Last's p. 587)
The superior brachium mediates conscious vision

The superior brachium mediates light reflexes, through the superior colliculus and pretectal nuclei. Conscious vision depends on the lateral geniculate body and optic radiation.
So a lesion of the radiation causes blindness with intact pupillary reflexes. (Last's p. 587)
Lies below the pulvinar on the posterior surface of the thalamus

The lateral geniculate body is a small elevation below the pulvinar on the posterior surface of the thalamus, found by following the optic tract back.
The medial geniculate body lies medial to it. (Last's p. 587)
Has six layers

The lateral geniculate body has six layers. Crossed fibres end in layers 1, 4 and 6, uncrossed fibres in layers 2, 3 and 5.
Each layer receives from one eye only. (Last's p. 587)
Receives uncrossed fibres in layers 1, 4 and 6

Uncrossed (temporal) fibres end in layers 2, 3 and 5. Crossed (nasal) fibres end in 1, 4 and 6.
"Crossed = 1, 4, 6." (Last's p. 587)
Projects to the visual cortex via the superior brachium

The lateral geniculate body projects to the visual cortex through the optic radiation (geniculocalcarine tract).
The superior brachium carries reflex fibres from the optic tract to the superior colliculus and pretectum. (Last's p. 587)
The superior colliculi are united by the posterior commissure

The two superior colliculi are united by the posterior commissure at the entrance to the aqueduct.
The posterior commissure also carries pretectal fibres for the consensual light reflex. (Last's p. 587-8)
Pupillary light reflex fibres pass bilaterally to the pretectal nuclei

Light reflex fibres from each eye pass to both pretectal nuclei. That is why light shone in one eye constricts both pupils (direct and consensual reflexes).
The bilateral connection continues: each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. (Last's p. 587-8)
Pupillary light reflex fibres synapse in the superior colliculus

Pupillary light reflex fibres do not synapse in the superior colliculus; they go to the pretectal nucleus.
The superior colliculus serves reflex movements of the head and eyes towards light. (Last's p. 587-8)
An Argyll Robertson pupil contracts to light but not to accommodation

An Argyll Robertson pupil loses its contraction to light but still contracts to accommodation and convergence ("light-near dissociation").
It is classically seen in neurosyphilis and is attributed to a pretectal lesion. (Last's p. 587-8)
Lies in the tegmentum under the upper and lateral margin of the superior colliculus

The pretectal nucleus lies in the tegmentum under the upper and lateral margin of the superior colliculus, at the junction of midbrain and diencephalon.
It receives light reflex fibres through the superior brachium. (Last's p. 587-8)
Sends light impulses to each Edinger-Westphal nucleus

Each pretectal nucleus sends light impulses to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, partly crossing in the posterior commissure. This gives the consensual light reflex.
Both pupils therefore constrict equally to light in either eye. (Last's p. 587-8)
Is the site of the lesion producing an Argyll Robertson pupil

A pretectal lesion abolishes the light reflex but spares accommodation, whose pathway bypasses the pretectum. This produces the Argyll Robertson pupil.
The same light-near dissociation occurs in Parinaud's syndrome. (Last's p. 587-8)
Sends fibres down as the tectospinal tract

The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus, not the pretectal nucleus.
It mediates reflex turning of the head in response to visual stimuli. (Last's p. 587-8)

questions.s: Components of the limbic system listed by Last's include:
o: The septal and piriform areas near the lamina terminalis

Last's lists the septal and piriform areas near the lamina terminalis as components of the limbic system.
The septal area is linked to the hippocampus through the fornix. (Last's p. 588-9)
The insula

Last's includes the insula in the limbic system, along with the uncus and the cingulate and parahippocampal gyri.
The insula is concerned with visceral sensation and emotion. (Last's p. 588-9)
The mammillary body

The mammillary body is a limbic component, along with the hippocampus, fimbria and fornix.
It is a relay in the Papez circuit. (Last's p. 588-9)
The claustrum

The claustrum is not listed as part of the limbic system; Last's says its significance is unknown.
It lies between the external and extreme capsules. (Last's p. 588-9)
It is an elongated extension of the white matter of the brain

The olfactory tract is an elongated extension of the white matter of the brain, like the optic nerve.
It is not a peripheral nerve in the usual sense. (Last's p. 588-9)
Its posterior end is expanded as the olfactory bulb

The olfactory bulb is the expanded anterior end of the olfactory tract.
The bulb lies on the cribriform plate. (Last's p. 588-9)
The second neuron reaches the cortex without thalamic relay

The second neuron of the olfactory pathway (the mitral cell) reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay. Last's calls this unique among the senses.
Every other sensory pathway relays in the thalamus. (Last's p. 588-9)
Its fibres reach the uncus through the posterior perforated substance

Olfactory fibres reach the uncus by passing across the anterior perforated substance (the lateral olfactory stria).
The posterior perforated substance is between the cerebral peduncles. (Last's p. 588-9)
It is the hippocampal sulcus projected into the floor of the inferior horn

The hippocampus is formed by the hippocampal sulcus rolled into the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.
Its curved shape gave it the name "seahorse". (Last's p. 589)
The alveus is a thin film of white matter on its ventricular surface

The alveus is a thin film of white matter on the ventricular surface of the hippocampus. Its fibres thicken medially to form the fimbria.
The fimbria then continues as the crus of the fornix. (Last's p. 589)
The pes hippocampi is its posterior part

The pes hippocampi is the anterior part of the hippocampus, with ridges like the knuckles of a clenched fist.
The hippocampus narrows posteriorly as it curves up under the splenium. (Last's p. 589)
The dentate gyrus lies between the fimbria and the cingulate gyrus

The dentate gyrus lies between the fimbria and the parahippocampal gyrus.
It is a notched strip of grey matter visible when the fimbria is lifted. (Last's p. 589)
Is the great efferent pathway from the hippocampus

The fornix is the great efferent pathway from the hippocampus. Hippocampal output runs through the alveus and fimbria into the fornix.
Its main targets are the mammillary bodies and the septal nuclei. (Last's p. 589)
Its commissure is really a chiasma

The commissure of the fornix (hippocampal commissure) is really a chiasma: an association tract linking the two hippocampi rather than a true commissure between symmetrical cortical areas.
It lies beneath the splenium. (Last's p. 589)
Its body lies above the corpus callosum

The body of the fornix lies beneath the corpus callosum, attached to it by the septum pellucidum in front.
It forms part of the roof of the body of the lateral ventricle medially. (Last's p. 589)
Its anterior columns form the posterior margins of the interventricular foramina

The anterior columns of the fornix form the anterior margins of the interventricular foramina. The anterior pole of the thalamus forms the posterior margin.
A colloid cyst sits just behind the columns, between the foramina. (Last's p. 589)

questions.s: The columns of the fornix and Papez circuit:
o: The columns pass both anterior and posterior to the anterior commissure

The columns of the fornix split around the anterior commissure. Precommissural fibres pass in front of it to the septal nuclei; postcommissural fibres pass behind it to the mammillary body and thalamus.
Most fibres are postcommissural. (Last's p. 589)
The precommissural fibres pass to nuclei within the septum pellucidum

Precommissural fibres pass to the septal nuclei near the lamina terminalis, not to nuclei within the septum pellucidum.
The septum pellucidum is a thin membrane with few or no neurons. (Last's p. 589)
The mamillothalamic tract runs in the lateral wall of the third ventricle

The mammillothalamic tract runs up in the lateral wall of the third ventricle to the anterior pole of the thalamus (the anterior nucleus).
It is a key link in the Papez circuit. (Last's p. 589)
The anterior thalamic neurons project to the parahippocampal gyrus

The anterior thalamic neurons project through the internal capsule to the cingulate gyrus, not to the parahippocampal gyrus.
The cingulate then connects back via the cingulum to the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampus. (Last's p. 589)
Is a thin film of grey matter on the upper surface of the corpus callosum

The induseum griseum is a thin film of grey matter on the upper surface of the corpus callosum.
It is a vestigial part of the hippocampal formation. (Last's p. 589)
Overlies the medial and lateral longitudinal striae

The medial and lateral longitudinal striae run beneath the induseum griseum. Last's regards them as aberrant fibres of the fornix.
They pass back to the hippocampus. (Last's p. 589)
Lies on the under surface of the corpus callosum

The induseum griseum lies on the upper surface of the corpus callosum, not the under surface.
The under surface is related to the fornix and septum pellucidum. (Last's p. 589)
Contains striae that are aberrant fibres of the cingulum

Last's describes the longitudinal striae as aberrant fibres of the fornix, not the cingulum.
The cingulum lies in the cingulate gyrus, above the callosal sulcus. (Last's p. 589)
A choroid plexus forms where ependyma contacts pia with no nervous tissue between

A choroid plexus forms where ependyma contacts pia with no nervous tissue between. Capillaries in the pia invaginate the thin wall to form the plexus.
This occurs along the choroid fissure and in the roofs of the third and fourth ventricles. (Last's p. 589-90)
The lateral ventricle plexuses secrete the bulk of the CSF

The large, highly vascular plexuses of the lateral ventricles secrete the bulk of the CSF. The fourth ventricle plexus contributes little.
The glomus in the atrium is the largest part. (Last's p. 589-90)
The fourth ventricle plexus is continuous with the third ventricle plexus

The fourth ventricle plexus is separate from the third ventricle plexus and makes only a small contribution.
The third and lateral ventricle plexuses are continuous through the interventricular foramina. (Last's p. 589-90)
The third ventricle comes to the surface in its floor

The third ventricle comes to the surface in its roof, where the ependyma is invaginated by two choroid plexuses.
The floor is formed by the hypothalamic structures. (Last's p. 589-90)
The central canal extends into the upper end of the filum terminale

The central canal of the cord extends down into the upper end of the filum terminale.
It may dilate slightly in the conus as the terminal ventricle. (Last's p. 589-90)
The midline ventricles are symmetrical

The midline ventricles (third ventricle, aqueduct and fourth ventricle) are symmetrical.
Midline shift of these on imaging therefore indicates a mass. (Last's p. 589-90)
Asymmetry of the lateral ventricles is abnormal

Asymmetry of the lateral ventricles, especially of the posterior horns, is the rule, not an abnormality.
The posterior horn may even be absent on one side. (Last's p. 589-90)
Apertures exist in the roof of the third ventricle

The only apertures of the ventricular system are in the roof of the fourth ventricle (median and lateral apertures).
The third ventricle has no openings to the subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 589-90)
It is a C-shaped slit on the medial surface of the hemisphere

The choroid fissure is a C-shaped slit on the medial surface of the hemisphere, curving around the thalamus and the tail of the caudate.
It runs from the interventricular foramen into the inferior horn. (Last's p. 590)
It is the medial wall of the body and inferior horn

The choroid fissure, where pia meets ependyma, forms the medial wall of the body and inferior horn of the lateral ventricle and admits the choroid plexus.
In the body it lies between the fornix and thalamus. (Last's p. 590)
It extends into the anterior horn

The choroid fissure is limited anteriorly by the interventricular foramen, so neither the fissure nor the plexus extends into the anterior horn.
The posterior horn also lacks plexus. (Last's p. 590)
It forms the lateral wall of the inferior horn

The inferior horn is closed laterally by the tapetum. The choroid fissure forms its medial wall.
The fimbria and stria terminalis border the fissure in the temporal horn. (Last's p. 590)
The calcarine sulcus

The calcarine sulcus indents the medial wall of the posterior horn as the calcar avis.
A large calcar avis can obliterate the horn. (Last's p. 590)
The collateral sulcus

The collateral sulcus indents the floor of the inferior horn (and atrium) as the collateral eminence.
It lies lateral to the hippocampus. (Last's p. 590)
The central sulcus

The central sulcus does not indent the lateral ventricle. The sulci that do are the hippocampal, calcarine and collateral sulci.
Each is deep enough to bulge into the ventricle. (Last's p. 590)
The cingulate sulcus

The cingulate sulcus does not indent the ventricle.
The corpus callosum lies between the cingulate gyrus and the ventricle. (Last's p. 590)

questions.s: The anterior horn and body of the lateral ventricle:
o: The anterior horn is bounded by the forceps minor

The anterior horn is bounded in front and above by the forceps minor, fibres from the genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum.
Its roof is the corpus callosum. (Last's p. 590)
The head of the caudate lies in its floor

The head of the caudate nucleus lies in the floor (lateral wall) of the anterior horn, bulging in and meeting the roof laterally.
So the horn is triangular in coronal section. (Last's p. 590)
The septum pellucidum separates the floor from the roof laterally

The septum pellucidum separates the floor from the roof medially, forming the medial wall of the anterior horn.
Laterally the caudate head meets the roof directly. (Last's p. 590)
The interventricular foramen lies in front of the anterior column of the fornix

The interventricular foramen lies behind the anterior column of the fornix, between it and the anterior pole of the thalamus.
It links the lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. (Last's p. 590)

questions.s: The floor of the body of the lateral ventricle:
o: Is formed by the thalamus and body of caudate

The floor of the body of the lateral ventricle is formed by the thalamus medially and the body of the caudate laterally, with the thalamostriate groove between.
The choroid plexus lies along the medial edge, at the choroid fissure. (Last's p. 590)
A band of white matter running the whole length of the caudate lies in the thalamostriate groove

A band of white matter runs the whole length of the caudate in the thalamostriate groove, from the amygdaloid body at the tail to the anterior perforated substance at the head. It is usually called the stria terminalis.
It accompanies the thalamostriate vein. (Last's p. 590)
The thalamostriate vein runs in the roof

The thalamostriate vein runs in the groove in the floor, not in the roof.
It joins the choroidal vein at the interventricular foramen to form the internal cerebral vein. (Last's p. 590)
The roof is formed by the septum pellucidum alone

The roof of the body is formed by the corpus callosum. The septum pellucidum and the crus and body of the fornix lie medially.
The septum forms the medial wall, not the roof. (Last's p. 590)
It is the most variably developed and may be absent

The posterior horn is the most variably developed part of the lateral ventricle and may be absent, obliterated by a large calcar avis.
Asymmetry is common and not pathological. (Last's p. 590-1)
The bulb of the posterior horn is formed by the forceps major

The bulb of the posterior horn is the upper convexity on the medial wall, formed by the forceps major (splenial fibres of the corpus callosum).
The calcar avis lies below it. (Last's p. 590-1)
The calcar avis is the upper convexity on the medial wall

The calcar avis is the lower convexity on the medial wall, formed by the calcarine sulcus. The bulb, formed by the forceps major, is the upper one.
"Bulb above, calcar below." (Last's p. 590-1)
The optic radiation lies in the medial wall

The optic radiation lies against the tapetum in the lateral wall of the posterior horn, not the medial wall.
Lateral approaches to the horn therefore risk the radiation. (Last's p. 590-1)
It is the largest horn

Last's describes the inferior horn, in the temporal lobe, as the largest horn of the lateral ventricle.
It extends forward to within about 2.5 cm of the temporal pole. (Last's p. 591-2)
The hippocampus forms the medial part of its floor

The hippocampus forms the medial part of the floor of the inferior horn, with the collateral eminence laterally.
The pes hippocampi lies at its front end. (Last's p. 591-2)
The tail of the caudate lies in its floor

The tail of the caudate lies in the roof of the inferior horn, not the floor.
It ends at the amygdala, at the tip of the horn. (Last's p. 591-2)
The fimbria forms the upper lip of the choroid fissure here

In the inferior horn the fimbria forms the lower lip of the choroid fissure; the stria terminalis lies above. In the body the fornix forms the lower lip and the thalamus the upper.
The fimbria is continuous with the fornix around the curve of the ventricle. (Last's p. 591-2)

questions.s: The C-shape of the lateral ventricle:
o: Structures around the convexity appear in the roof of the body and floor of the inferior horn

Structures curving around the outside (convexity) of the C-shaped ventricle, the corpus callosum and fornix above and the fimbria and hippocampus below, form the roof of the body and the floor of the inferior horn.
The rule follows from the ventricle being bent around the thalamus. (Last's p. 591-2)
The amygdala lies to the lateral side of the anterior perforated substance

The amygdala lies lateral to the anterior perforated substance, bulging into the roof at the tip of the inferior horn.
It is deep to the uncus. (Last's p. 591-2)
Structures in the concavity appear in the roof of the body

Structures in the concavity of the C (caudate and thalamus, stria terminalis) appear in the floor of the body and the roof of the inferior horn.
So the caudate is in the floor of the body but the roof of the inferior horn. (Last's p. 591-2)
The internal capsule lies outside the concavity of the caudate

The internal capsule lies within the concavity of the C-shaped caudate nucleus.
The caudate wraps around the lateral and upper side of the capsule and thalamus. (Last's p. 591-2)

questions.s: The anterior wall and floor of the third ventricle:
o: The lamina terminalis extends from the rostrum of the corpus callosum to the chiasma

The lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle, extending from the rostrum of the corpus callosum down to the optic chiasma.
It is the original front end of the neural tube. (Last's p. 592-3)
The anterior commissure lies in the upper part of the lamina terminalis

The anterior commissure lies in the upper part of the lamina terminalis, joining the two piriform (olfactory) areas.
It also links the middle and inferior temporal gyri. (Last's p. 592-3)
The anterior commissure joins the two cingulate gyri

The anterior commissure joins the two piriform areas, not the cingulate gyri.
The cingulate gyri are linked by the corpus callosum. (Last's p. 592-3)
The floor ends at the anterior perforated substance

The floor of the third ventricle extends back as far as the posterior perforated substance (and tegmentum of the midbrain).
It includes the chiasma, tuber cinereum, infundibulum and mammillary bodies. (Last's p. 592-3)

questions.s: The septum pellucidum and third ventricle (Last's):
o: The cavum septi pellucidi is lined with pia, not ependyma

The cavum septi pellucidi lies between the two layers of the septum pellucidum, which are parts of the medial walls of the hemispheres. It lies outside the ventricles, so it is lined with pia, not ependyma.
Last's says the name "fifth ventricle" is a misnomer. (Last's p. 593)
The cavum septi pellucidi communicates with the ventricular system

The cavum septi pellucidi has no connexion with the ventricular system, which is why Last's says "fifth ventricle" should be avoided.
It is a normal variant in many brains. (Last's p. 593)
The interthalamic adhesion is not a commissure

The interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia) is not a commissure: there is no significant interchange of fibres across it.
It is simply a fusion of the two thalami across the third ventricle. (Last's p. 593)
The interthalamic adhesion is present in about 20% of brains

The interthalamic adhesion is present in about 60 percent (two-thirds) of brains, not 20 percent.
Its absence is a normal variant. (Last's p. 593)
The hypothalamus lies below the hypothalamic groove

The hypothalamus lies below the hypothalamic groove (sulcus) in the lateral wall of the third ventricle, and includes the floor.
The thalamus lies above the groove. (Last's p. 594)
The subthalamic nucleus lies on the medial side of the internal capsule

The subthalamic nucleus lies on the medial side of the internal capsule, adjacent to (above) the substantia nigra.
It is the target of deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease. (Last's p. 594)
The subthalamic nucleus belongs functionally to the limbic system

The subthalamic nucleus belongs functionally to the basal nuclei, not the limbic system.
Its destruction causes hemiballismus on the opposite side. (Last's p. 594)
Supraoptic axons control the anterior lobe through the portal vessels

Supraoptic and paraventricular axons run down the hypothalamohypophysial tract to the posterior lobe. The anterior lobe is controlled through the portal vessels by releasing hormones from other nuclei.
Posterior = nerve; anterior = blood. (Last's p. 594)

questions.s: The roof of the third ventricle (Last's):
o: The medullary striae join posteriorly in the habenular commissure

The medullary striae of the thalamus run along the upper margin of the thalamus and join posteriorly in the habenular commissure.
They carry fibres from the septal area to the habenular nuclei. (Last's p. 594-5)
The habenular commissure is probably olfactory

Last's says the habenular commissure is probably olfactory in function, like the anterior commissure.
It lies in the upper lamina of the pineal stalk. (Last's p. 594-5)
The suprapineal recess lies within the pineal stalk

The recess within the pineal stalk is the pineal recess. The suprapineal recess lies above, between the pineal and the habenular commissure (beneath the tela choroidea).
Both are extensions of the third ventricle. (Last's p. 594-5)
The roof is a thick layer of nervous tissue

The roof of the third ventricle is a thin layer of pia lined with ependyma (tela choroidea), not nervous tissue.
Two choroid plexuses hang from it. (Last's p. 594-5)
Lies above the superior colliculi, below the splenium

The pineal body lies above the superior colliculi, between the backs of the thalami and below the splenium of the corpus callosum.
The great cerebral vein runs just above it. (Last's p. 595)
Lacks a blood-brain barrier

The pineal is one of the circumventricular organs that lack a blood–brain barrier.
This lets it release melatonin directly into the blood. (Last's p. 595)
Is normally calcified on radiographs before age 20

Last's says the pineal normally calcifies after the age of forty, when it shows on radiographs.
Calcification before about age ten may suggest a tumour. (Last's p. 595)
Secretes melatonin with a gonadotrophic action

Melatonin has an antigonadotrophic action.
That is why destructive pineal tumours in children can cause precocious puberty. (Last's p. 595)

questions.s: Regarding the pineal stalk and thalamus:
o: The posterior commissure connects the two superior colliculi

The posterior commissure connects the two superior colliculi and lies above the entrance to the aqueduct.
It carries light reflex and vertical gaze fibres. (Last's p. 595)
The pineal recess lies between the habenular and posterior commissures

The pineal stalk is hollowed into the pineal recess between the habenular commissure (above) and the posterior commissure (below).
The suprapineal recess lies above the habenular commissure. (Last's p. 595)
The neothalamus lies on the medial side of the thalamus

The neothalamus lies on the lateral side of the thalamus, connected with the neocortex.
The more ancient parts (anterior and medial) lie medially. (Last's p. 595)
The thalamus is part of the cerebral hemisphere

The thalamus is part of the wall of the diencephalon, not the cerebral hemisphere (telencephalon).
It forms the upper lateral wall of the third ventricle. (Last's p. 595)
The medial walls of the two thalami lie parallel

The medial walls of the two thalami lie parallel, forming the lateral walls of the third ventricle, and are joined by the interthalamic adhesion in about two-thirds of cases.
The ventricle is a narrow slit between them. (Last's p. 595-6)
The pulvinar is the large posterior convexity

The pulvinar is the large posterior convexity of the thalamus. The lateral geniculate body bulges from its lateral part.
The pulvinar overhangs the superior colliculus. (Last's p. 595-6)
The anterior pole is large and the pulvinar small

The thalamus has a small, blunt anterior pole and a large pulvinar behind.
The anterior pole forms the back of the interventricular foramen. (Last's p. 595-6)
The medial geniculate body relays through the retrolentiform internal capsule

The medial geniculate body relays auditory fibres through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule.
The retrolentiform part carries the optic radiation from the lateral geniculate body. (Last's p. 595-6)
The lateral surface is bevelled by the internal capsule

The lateral surface of the thalamus is bevelled by the internal capsule, which lies against it.
The posterior limb lies between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus. (Last's p. 596)
The anterior pole lies at the interventricular foramen

The anterior pole of the thalamus lies at the interventricular foramen, covered with ependyma.
It forms the posterior boundary of the foramen. (Last's p. 596)
The inferior surface is wider than the superior

The inferior surface of the thalamus is narrower than the superior surface.
The inferior surface rests on the hypothalamus and subthalamus. (Last's p. 596)
The superior surface is entirely covered with ependyma

The superior surface lies on the external surface of the brain (beneath the fornix and tela choroidea) and is covered with pia. Only a lateral strip, in the floor of the lateral ventricle, is covered with ependyma.
That lateral strip lies between the choroid fissure and the thalamostriate groove. (Last's p. 596)
The ventroposterior part of the lateral nuclei receives the medial and spinal lemnisci

The ventroposterior part of the lateral nuclear group receives the medial and spinal lemnisci and projects to the sensory cortex.
VPL serves the body, VPM the face. (Last's p. 596)
Parts of the lateral nucleus receive from the dentate nucleus and globus pallidus

Parts of the lateral nucleus receive from the dentate nucleus and the globus pallidus and project to the motor areas of the cortex.
These are the ventral lateral and ventral anterior nuclei. (Last's p. 596)
The anterior nucleus receives the mamillothalamic tract and projects to the frontal eye field

The anterior nucleus receives the mammillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus, not to the frontal eye field.
This is part of the Papez circuit. (Last's p. 596)
The medial geniculate is concerned with vision

The medial geniculate body is concerned with hearing. The lateral geniculate body is concerned with vision.
"Lateral = light; medial = music." (Last's p. 596)
It is two layers of pia lying in contact

The tela choroidea consists of two layers of pia lying in contact. They are trapped because the fornix and corpus callosum project backward over the diencephalon.
It forms the roof of the third ventricle and carries the internal cerebral veins. (Last's p. 596-7)
It forms a triangular pouch with its apex forwards

The tela choroidea is a triangular double layer of pia with its apex forward at the interventricular foramina.
Its lateral edges project into the choroid fissures as the plexuses of the lateral ventricles. (Last's p. 596-7)
Its base is closed

The base of the triangle is open posteriorly, where its two layers part.
This open base lies beneath the splenium, where the great cerebral vein emerges. (Last's p. 596-7)
The upper layer passes down over the back of the midbrain

It is the lower layer that passes down over the back of the midbrain. The upper layer passes forward around the splenium.
The two layers separate at the open base. (Last's p. 596-7)
The neural tube cavity reaches the surface at two places, both dorsal

The cavity of the neural tube reaches the surface (becomes covered only by ependyma and pia) at two places, both dorsal: the roof of the forebrain and the roof of the hindbrain.
These are the sites of the choroid plexuses. (Last's p. 597)
The anterior choroidal artery feeds the lateral ventricle plexus at its lateral extremity

The anterior choroidal artery feeds the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle at its lateral extremity, which becomes the tip of the inferior horn as the hemisphere grows.
So the anterior choroidal artery enters the inferior end of the choroid fissure in the adult. (Last's p. 597)
The corpus callosum grows first backwards then forwards

The corpus callosum grows first forward (forming the rostrum and genu), then backward (body and splenium).
This explains why it begins at the anterior commissure. (Last's p. 597)
The fornix is composed of commissural fibres

The fornix is composed of association fibres, linking the hippocampus with the mammillary body and septum within the same hemisphere.
Only its small hippocampal commissure crosses. (Last's p. 597)
The cerebral vesicles grow caudally, then ventrally, then forwards

The cerebral vesicles grow first caudally, then ventrally, then forward, giving the C-shape of the lateral ventricle, caudate and fornix.
The temporal lobe is the forward-growing end. (Last's p. 598-9)
The internal capsule almost separates caudate from lentiform nucleus

Fibres of the internal capsule cut through the corpus striatum and almost separate the caudate from the lentiform nucleus.
Grey bridges remain across the anterior limb, giving the striated look. (Last's p. 598-9)
The corpus striatum develops in the roof of the cerebral vesicle

The corpus striatum develops in the floor of the cerebral vesicle.
The roof is thin and forms the choroid fissure. (Last's p. 598-9)
The choroid fissure represents the original ventral floor plate

The choroid fissure represents the original dorsal roof plate of the neural tube, not the ventral floor plate.
That is why the choroid plexus, a roof structure, is attached there. (Last's p. 598-9)
The insula and piriform area are remnants of the archaeopallium

The insula and piriform area are remnants of the archaeopallium (ancient cortex). The huge neopallium has grown over and buried the insula.
The olfactory cortex is archaeopallium. (Last's p. 599)
The archaeocerebellum was mainly vestibular

The archaeocerebellum was mainly vestibular in its connections, matching the smell-dominated archaeopallium.
The flocculonodular lobe is its remnant in the adult. (Last's p. 599)
The corpus callosum is the commissure of the archaeopallium

The corpus callosum is the commissure of the neopallium. The anterior and posterior (hippocampal) commissures unite the archaeopallium.
Its size reflects the expansion of the neocortex. (Last's p. 599)
The red nucleus appeared with the archaeopallium

The red nucleus appeared with the neopallium, as did the neocerebellum and the olivary nucleus.
These structures are linked to neocortical motor control. (Last's p. 599)
The basilar divides at the upper border of the pons

The basilar artery ends at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
III emerges between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries just below. (Last's p. 599-600)
The posterior communicating runs through the interpeduncular cistern

The posterior communicating artery runs forward through the interpeduncular cistern to join the internal carotid artery near the anterior perforated substance.
III lies just below and lateral to it. (Last's p. 599-600)
The anterior communicating lies in the interpeduncular cistern

The anterior communicating artery lies in the chiasmatic cistern, in front of the chiasma.
The interpeduncular cistern contains the back of the circle and the basilar bifurcation. (Last's p. 599-600)
The circle encircles the mamillary bodies

Last's says the circle encircles only the optic chiasma and pituitary stalk.
The mammillary bodies lie at or behind its posterior edge. (Last's p. 599-600)
Rupture of circle aneurysms causes about 90% of subarachnoid haemorrhages

About 90 percent of subarachnoid haemorrhages come from ruptured aneurysms of the circle of Willis.
The rest are mostly from arteriovenous malformations. (Last's p. 599-600)
Aneurysms are commoner on the carotid part of the circle

Congenital (berry) aneurysms are more common on the carotid (anterior) part of the circle, especially at branch points.
The anterior communicating artery is the commonest site. (Last's p. 599-600)
They are commonest where the tunica intima is weakest

Aneurysms are commonest where the tunica media is weakest, at branching points.
The intima is not the weak layer; the media defect allows the wall to balloon. (Last's p. 599-600)
Arteries entering the brain anastomose freely at precapillary level

Arteries entering the brain substance are end arteries; they do not anastomose freely at precapillary level.
That is why occlusion of a perforating artery causes a localised infarct. (Last's p. 599-600)
The anterior choroidal does not supply cortex

The anterior choroidal artery supplies deep structures (choroid plexus, optic tract, lateral geniculate body, posterior part of the internal capsule) but no cortex.
That is why Last's calls it the fourth artery to the cerebrum but not a cortical artery. (Last's p. 600)
Surface vessels have sympathetic innervation that is lost intracortically

The larger surface arteries of the brain carry a sympathetic plexus, but once they enter the cortex they are not innervated.
Cerebral blood flow is regulated mainly by local metabolic and autoregulatory factors. (Last's p. 600)
The anterior choroidal arises from the anterior cerebral

The anterior choroidal artery arises from the termination of the internal carotid, or sometimes from the middle cerebral or posterior communicating artery.
It does not come from the anterior cerebral artery. (Last's p. 600)
The perforating branches anastomose with each other

The perforating (central) branches are invariably end arteries; they do not anastomose with each other.
Their occlusion therefore causes lacunar infarcts. (Last's p. 600)

questions.s: Regions without a blood-brain barrier (Last's) include:
o: Posterior pituitary

The posterior pituitary lacks a blood–brain barrier, allowing vasopressin and oxytocin to enter the blood.
It is one of the circumventricular organs. (Last's p. 600)
Pineal body

The pineal body lacks a blood–brain barrier, so melatonin passes freely into the blood.
It is another circumventricular organ. (Last's p. 600)
Median eminence

The median eminence lacks a barrier, so that hypothalamic releasing hormones can enter the portal vessels.
This is how the hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary. (Last's p. 600)
Choroid plexus epithelium of the lateral ventricle

Last's list of regions without a barrier does not include the choroid plexus epithelium of the lateral ventricle; the fourth listed region is the area postrema.
The choroid plexus has its own blood–CSF barrier formed by the epithelial tight junctions. (Last's p. 600)

questions.s: Concerning the intracranial internal carotid artery and brain capillaries:
o: Gives off the ophthalmic artery after emerging from the cavernous sinus roof

The internal carotid artery gives off the ophthalmic artery just after it emerges through the roof of the cavernous sinus, then curls back on the roof.
The ophthalmic artery enters the optic canal below the optic nerve. (Last's p. 600)
Divides at the anterior perforated substance

The internal carotid divides at the anterior perforated substance into the middle and anterior cerebral arteries.
Its terminal part gives the posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries first. (Last's p. 600)
Lies on the back half of the cavernous sinus roof after curling back

After curling back, the internal carotid lies on the front half of the roof of the cavernous sinus.
It then ascends lateral to the optic chiasma. (Last's p. 600)
Brain capillaries are fenestrated with few tight junctions

Brain capillaries lack fenestrations and have abundant tight junctions. These features form the blood–brain barrier.
Fenestrated capillaries are found only in the circumventricular organs. (Last's p. 600)
Is the largest and most direct branch of the internal carotid

The middle cerebral artery is the largest and most direct continuation of the internal carotid, so it is the artery most subject to embolism.
Emboli from the heart or carotid tend to go straight into it. (Last's p. 600)
Supplies the insula and overlying opercula

The middle cerebral artery runs deep in the lateral sulcus and supplies the insula and the overlying opercula before reaching the lateral surface.
Its branches emerge from the sulcus to fan out. (Last's p. 600)
Supplies the superior frontal gyrus

The middle cerebral territory falls short of the borders of the lateral surface by about one gyrus: it does not reach the superior frontal or inferior temporal gyri.
The superior frontal gyrus is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. (Last's p. 600)
Supplies the motor area for the leg and perineum

The motor areas for the leg and perineum lie on the medial surface (paracentral lobule) in anterior cerebral territory.
Middle cerebral occlusion therefore spares the leg relatively. (Last's p. 600)
Passes forwards above the optic nerve

The anterior cerebral artery runs forward and medially above the optic nerve to the longitudinal fissure.
The anterior communicating artery joins the two arteries there. (Last's p. 600)
Supplies the medial surface above the corpus callosum back to the parieto-occipital sulcus

The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface above the corpus callosum back to the parieto-occipital sulcus, plus the orbital surface and a strip over the superior border.
This includes the leg and perineal motor and sensory areas. (Last's p. 600)
Supplies the inferior temporal gyrus

The inferior temporal gyrus is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery.
The anterior cerebral supplies only frontal and parietal regions. (Last's p. 600)
Never arises from the opposite carotid

Occasionally both anterior cerebral arteries arise from one carotid by a common stem.
So "never" is wrong; variations of the circle are common. (Last's p. 600)

questions.s: Concerning internal carotid stenosis or occlusion (Last's):
o: It may cause blindness in one eye with contralateral hemiplegia

Internal carotid stenosis or occlusion may cause blindness in one eye (ophthalmic territory) with contralateral hemiplegia (anterior and middle cerebral territories).
Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) is a warning sign. (Last's p. 600)
It may be clinically silent

Carotid occlusion may be clinically silent, because collateral flow through the arterial circle can maintain the territory.
The adequacy of the circle varies between individuals. (Last's p. 600)
The typical combination is blindness in one eye with ipsilateral hemiplegia

The typical combination is blindness in one eye with contralateral hemiplegia. The eye is on the same side as the carotid lesion; the hemiplegia is on the opposite side.
This "crossed" pattern points to the carotid. (Last's p. 600)
Micturition and defecation areas lie in middle cerebral territory

The cortical areas for micturition and defecation lie on the medial surface, in anterior cerebral territory.
Anterior cerebral occlusion may cause incontinence. (Last's p. 600)
Supplies the cerebral peduncle and optic tract as it curls round the peduncle

As it curls round the cerebral peduncle, the posterior cerebral artery supplies the peduncle and the optic tract.
It then runs on to the occipital and inferior temporal cortex. (Last's p. 601)
Supplies the inferior temporal gyrus

The posterior cerebral artery supplies the inferior temporal gyrus and a strip of lateral occipital cortex, as well as the medial occipital lobe.
So its occlusion may affect memory and colour recognition as well as vision. (Last's p. 601)
Has the macular visual cortex always wholly within its territory

Middle cerebral branches sometimes supply the macular area at the occipital pole, which accounts for macular sparing in posterior cerebral occlusion.
So the macular cortex is not always wholly in posterior cerebral territory. (Last's p. 601)
Arising from the internal carotid is an acquired anomaly

A posterior cerebral artery arising from the internal carotid (fetal PCA) is persistence of the primitive embryonic pattern, not an acquired anomaly.
In the embryo the posterior cerebral is a branch of the carotid. (Last's p. 601)
They enter through the anterior perforated substance from anterior and middle cerebrals

Striate branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries enter the brain through the anterior perforated substance.
They supply the basal nuclei and internal capsule. (Last's p. 601)
Medial striate branches supply the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule

The medial striate branches supply the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule.
The largest of them is Heubner's artery. (Last's p. 601)
Heubner's artery arises from the middle cerebral

Heubner's artery (the recurrent artery) arises from the anterior cerebral artery.
It runs back above the anterior cerebral to the anterior perforated substance. (Last's p. 601)
Heubner's artery is absent in about 30%

Heubner's artery is absent in about 3 percent of brains, not 30 percent.
The factor of ten is the trap. (Last's p. 601)
They arise from the middle cerebral and anterior choroidal arteries

The lateral striate arteries come from the middle cerebral and anterior choroidal arteries.
One from the middle cerebral is the "artery of cerebral haemorrhage". (Last's p. 601)
One of them is "the artery of cerebral haemorrhage"

Last's calls one of the lateral striate branches of the middle cerebral the "artery of cerebral haemorrhage" (Charcot's artery).
Its rupture causes capsular haemorrhage. (Last's p. 601)
They arise from the posterior cerebral artery

Posterior cerebral branches enter the posterior perforated substance to supply the thalamus and midbrain. The lateral striate arteries come from the middle cerebral and anterior choroidal arteries.
Anterior perforated substance: striate arteries; posterior: thalamoperforators. (Last's p. 601)
Their occlusion typically causes ipsilateral hemiplegia

Occlusion of the lateral striate arteries typically causes contralateral hemiplegia, because the corticospinal fibres in the internal capsule have not yet crossed.
Lacunar infarcts in the capsule cause pure motor hemiplegia. (Last's p. 601)
Passes below the optic tract

The anterior choroidal artery runs back below the optic tract, supplying it on the way.
It then reaches the choroid fissure. (Last's p. 601)
Enters the choroid fissure at the tip of the inferior horn, just above the uncus

The anterior choroidal artery enters the choroid fissure at the tip of the inferior horn, just above the uncus.
It supplies the plexus of the inferior horn. (Last's p. 601)
Supplies the anterior limb of the internal capsule

The anterior choroidal artery supplies the posterior part of the internal capsule (lower posterior limb), not the anterior limb.
The anterior limb is supplied by Heubner's artery and the lateral striate arteries. (Last's p. 601)
Supplies the medial geniculate body

The anterior choroidal supplies the chiasma, optic tract and lateral geniculate body, not the medial geniculate body.
The medial geniculate is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery. (Last's p. 601)

questions.s: Effects of complete occlusion described by Last's:
o: Anterior cerebral distal to Heubner's artery affects only the opposite leg

Occlusion of the anterior cerebral artery beyond the origin of Heubner's artery spares the internal capsule, so only the opposite leg area of cortex is lost.
Proximal occlusion also affects the capsule. (Last's p. 601)
Middle cerebral occlusion may cause hemianopia from oedema compressing the optic radiation

Middle cerebral occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia and hemianaesthesia, plus hemianopia if oedema compresses the optic radiation.
The radiation itself lies at the edge of the territory. (Last's p. 601)
Posterior cerebral occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia

Posterior cerebral occlusion causes contralateral hemianopia and hemianaesthesia (from thalamic branches), with cerebral oedema, but not hemiplegia.
Hemiplegia is a feature of anterior choroidal or middle cerebral occlusion. (Last's p. 601)
Anterior choroidal occlusion spares vision

Anterior choroidal occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia.
The hemianopia comes from damage to the optic tract and lateral geniculate body. (Last's p. 601)
Cortical veins travel superficially in the arachnoid

Cortical veins travel superficially in the arachnoid, unlike the arteries, which run deep in the sulci.
The veins are exposed on the surface at operation. (Last's p. 602)
They enter sinuses obliquely against the bloodstream

Cortical veins enter the dural venous sinuses obliquely, against the direction of blood flow.
This oblique entry may act as a valve-like mechanism. (Last's p. 602)
Superior cerebral veins meeting a blood lake pass between the dural layers

When superior cerebral veins meet a venous lake (lacuna), they pass on its cerebral surface beneath the arachnoid, not between the dural layers.
Bridging veins can tear in head injury, causing subdural haematoma. (Last's p. 602)
The superficial middle cerebral vein drains into the transverse sinus
