The superficial middle cerebral vein drains into the cavernous sinus (or sphenoparietal sinus).
The inferior anastomotic vein connects it to the transverse sinus. (Last's p. 602)
The depths of the lateral sulcus and insula drain by the deep middle cerebral vein

The depths of the lateral sulcus and the insula drain by the deep middle cerebral vein, which joins the basal vein.
It runs with the middle cerebral artery. (Last's p. 602)
The anterior cerebral vein drains the orbital surface of the frontal lobe

The anterior cerebral vein drains the orbital surface of the frontal lobe and the medial surface in front, then joins the basal vein.
It accompanies the anterior cerebral artery. (Last's p. 602)
The anterior cerebral vein drains into the inferior sagittal sinus

The anterior cerebral vein joins the basal vein, not the inferior sagittal sinus.
The inferior sagittal sinus drains the medial surface and falx. (Last's p. 602)
The superior anastomotic vein empties into the transverse sinus

The superior anastomotic vein (Trolard) empties into the superior sagittal sinus. The inferior anastomotic vein (Labbé) empties into the transverse sinus.
"Superior to the superior; inferior to the transverse." (Last's p. 602)
Is formed from striate, deep middle cerebral and anterior cerebral veins

The basal vein (of Rosenthal) is formed at the anterior perforated substance by the striate, deep middle cerebral and anterior cerebral veins.
It drains the base of the brain. (Last's p. 603)
Passes round the peduncle below the optic tract

The basal vein passes back around the cerebral peduncle below the optic tract, together with IV and the posterior cerebral artery.
It ends in the great cerebral vein. (Last's p. 603)
Drains the upper parts of the basal ganglia

The basal vein drains only the lower parts of the basal ganglia. The upper parts drain to the internal cerebral vein (through the thalamostriate vein).
So the deep venous drainage is split between the two systems. (Last's p. 603)
Joins the straight sinus directly

The basal vein joins the great cerebral vein below the splenium, not the straight sinus directly.
The great vein then joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus. (Last's p. 603)
Is formed at the interventricular foramen

The internal cerebral vein is formed at the interventricular foramen by the union of the choroidal and thalamostriate veins.
The angle of union (venous angle) marks the foramen on angiography. (Last's p. 603)
Runs back in the tela choroidea

The internal cerebral veins run back in the tela choroidea above the third ventricle and unite as the great cerebral vein.
They lie in the roof of the third ventricle. (Last's p. 603)
Receives the septal veins directly in most cases

Last's says the septal veins usually join the thalamostriate vein rather than the internal cerebral vein directly.
The details vary between brains. (Last's p. 603)
Joins its fellow above the splenium

The two internal cerebral veins join beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum to form the great cerebral vein.
Above the splenium lies the inferior sagittal sinus. (Last's p. 603)

questions.s: The structure of the cerebral cortex (Last's):
o: Layer I is the plexiform layer

Layer I of the cortex is the plexiform (molecular) layer, with abundant fibres and few cells.
It lies just beneath the pia. (Last's p. 603)
Layer IV is the ganglionic layer

Layer IV is the internal granular layer. Layer V is the ganglionic (internal pyramidal) layer, containing the Betz cells in the motor cortex.
Layers from the surface: plexiform, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, ganglionic, multiform. (Last's p. 603)
The stria of Gennari is the external band of Baillarger

The stria of Gennari in the visual cortex is the external band of Baillarger, much thickened.
It lies in layer IV. (Last's p. 603)
Betz cells give rise to about 20% of corticospinal fibres

Betz cells give rise to no more than about 2 percent of corticospinal fibres.
Most corticospinal fibres come from smaller pyramidal cells. (Last's p. 603)
Sensory cortex has predominantly granular cells

Sensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, calcarine cortex) has predominantly granular cells and is called granular (koniocortex).
Motor cortex, by contrast, is agranular, with prominent pyramidal cells. (Last's p. 603)
Betz cells are in layer V of the precentral gyrus

Giant pyramidal Betz cells lie in layer V (the ganglionic layer) of the precentral gyrus.
They give rise to only about 2 percent of corticospinal fibres. (Last's p. 603)
CNS myelin is formed by Schwann cells

CNS myelin is formed by oligodendrocytes. Schwann cells form peripheral myelin.
One oligodendrocyte myelinates many axons; one Schwann cell myelinates one internode. (Last's p. 603)
Layer II is the external pyramidal layer

Layer II is the external granular layer. Layer III is the external pyramidal layer.
The six layers: plexiform, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, ganglionic, multiform. (Last's p. 603)
It extends from just above the tentorial aperture to C1

The brainstem runs from just above the tentorial aperture (the upper midbrain) down to C1 just below the foramen magnum.
The midbrain lies in the tentorial notch. (Last's p. 603-5)
The reticular formation continues into the spinal cord

The diffuse reticular formation runs through the whole brainstem and continues into the spinal cord.
It controls arousal, posture and vital functions. (Last's p. 603-5)
The vital centres are anatomically demonstrable nuclei

Last's says the vital (respiratory and cardiovascular) centres are not anatomically demonstrable as distinct nuclei; they are functional regions of the reticular formation.
This is a point Last's makes explicitly. (Last's p. 603-5)
Five sections are the minimum needed to understand it

Last's says a minimum of seven transverse sections is needed to understand the brainstem.
The levels run from the upper midbrain to the lower medulla. (Last's p. 603-5)
III and IV nuclei are in the midbrain

The oculomotor and trochlear nuclei lie in the midbrain, at the levels of the superior and inferior colliculi respectively.
These are the only cranial nerve motor nuclei in the midbrain. (Last's p. 603-5)
The trigeminal motor nucleus, VI and VII are in the pons

The trigeminal motor, abducent and facial nuclei lie in the pons.
The facial and abducent nuclei are in the lower pons; the trigeminal motor in the mid pons. (Last's p. 603-5)
The eighth nerve nuclei lie wholly in the medulla

The nuclei of VIII (cochlear and vestibular) overlap the pontomedullary junction, lying partly in each.
So "wholly in the medulla" is wrong. (Last's p. 603-5)
The trigeminal sensory nuclei are confined to pons and medulla

The trigeminal sensory nuclei extend through the midbrain (mesencephalic nucleus), pons (main sensory nucleus) and medulla (spinal nucleus).
They even continue into the upper cervical cord. (Last's p. 603-5)
Most of it lies in the posterior cranial fossa

Most of the midbrain lies in the posterior cranial fossa, extending from just above the dorsum sellae to the level of the petrous apices.
It passes through the tentorial notch. (Last's p. 606)
The tectum is the part dorsal to the aqueduct

The tectum is the part of the midbrain dorsal to the aqueduct, consisting of the superior and inferior colliculi.
The tegmentum and the cerebral peduncles lie in front. (Last's p. 606)
The medial geniculate body lies medial to the superior colliculus

The medial geniculate body lies lateral to each superior colliculus, connected to the inferior colliculus by the inferior brachium.
Despite its name, it is lateral to the colliculi. (Last's p. 606)
The superior cerebellar peduncles converge above the superior colliculi

The superior cerebellar peduncles converge below the inferior colliculi, entering the midbrain there.
They decussate at the level of the inferior colliculus. (Last's p. 606)

questions.s: The trochlear nerve is unique in that it:
o: Is the smallest cranial nerve

IV is the smallest cranial nerve, with about 3400 fibres.
It supplies only superior oblique. (Last's p. 606)
Is the only one emerging dorsally

IV is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the back (dorsum) of the brainstem, just behind the inferior colliculus.
All others emerge ventrally or laterally. (Last's p. 606)
Is the only one to decussate within the brainstem

IV is the only cranial nerve whose fibres decussate completely inside the brainstem, in the superior medullary velum.
So each nucleus supplies the opposite superior oblique. (Last's p. 606)
Is the only one passing between posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

III also passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, more medially than IV.
So this relation is not unique to IV. (Last's p. 606)
The trochlear nerve passes lateral to the oculomotor between the arteries

Both III and IV pass between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries; IV lies farther laterally as it winds around the peduncle.
III is closer to the midline at the interpeduncular fossa. (Last's p. 606)
The basal vein lies ventral to the optic tract

As the optic tract curls round the cerebral peduncle, the basal vein (and posterior communicating artery) lie ventral to it.
The basal vein runs back to the great cerebral vein. (Last's p. 606)
The posterior communicating artery lies dorsal to the optic tract

The posterior communicating artery lies ventral to the optic tract, not dorsal.
It runs forward below the tract to the internal carotid. (Last's p. 606)
The trochlear nerve enters the cavernous sinus above the free edge of the tentorium

IV runs just below the free edge of the tentorium, then pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus where the free and attached edges cross.
It is at risk when the tentorial edge is cut. (Last's p. 606)
At superior colliculus level the red nucleus is seen

A section at the level of the superior colliculus shows the red nucleus, with oculomotor fibres sweeping through it to emerge in the interpeduncular fossa.
The oculomotor nucleus lies in front of the aqueduct. (Last's p. 606-7)
At inferior colliculus level the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles is central

A section at the level of the inferior colliculus shows the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles centrally in the tegmentum.
The trochlear nucleus is also at this level. (Last's p. 606-7)
The substantia nigra belongs functionally to the limbic system

The substantia nigra belongs functionally to the basal nuclei, not the limbic system.
Its dopaminergic neurons project to the striatum. (Last's p. 606-7)
Parkinsonism follows loss of about 30% of nigral dopaminergic cells

Parkinsonism appears after loss of about 80 percent of nigral dopaminergic cells, not 30 percent.
The large reserve explains the long presymptomatic phase. (Last's p. 606-7)
The superior colliculus mediates general light reflexes

The superior colliculus mediates general reflexes to light, such as blinking and turning the head and eyes, through the tectobulbar and tectospinal tracts.
It does not mediate the pupillary light reflex. (Last's p. 606-7)
The inferior colliculus mediates sound reflexes

The inferior colliculus is a relay for reflex responses to sound, such as turning towards a noise.
It also relays auditory fibres to the medial geniculate body. (Last's p. 606-7)
The pretectal nuclei lie caudal to the superior colliculi

The pretectal nuclei lie just cranial (rostral) to the superior colliculi, at the junction of the midbrain and diencephalon.
They mediate the pupillary light reflex. (Last's p. 606-7)
The colliculi project via the medial longitudinal bundle only

The colliculi project mainly through the tectobulbar and tectospinal tracts, not through the medial longitudinal bundle only.
These tracts reach cranial nerve nuclei and the cervical cord. (Last's p. 606-7)
The oculomotor nucleus lies against the midline ventral to the aqueduct

The oculomotor nucleus lies against the midline, ventral to the aqueduct, in line with the other somatic motor nuclei (IV, VI and XII).
All four supply muscles derived from somites. (Last's p. 607)
The trochlear nucleus is at inferior colliculus level

The trochlear nucleus lies at the level of the inferior colliculus, caudal to the oculomotor nucleus.
It is continuous with the lower end of the oculomotor complex. (Last's p. 607)
The red nucleus lies dorsal to the oculomotor nucleus

The red nucleus lies ventral to the oculomotor nucleus, and III axons pass through it.
So a tegmental lesion can damage both. (Last's p. 607)
The red nucleus receives from the ipsilateral dentate nucleus

The red nucleus receives from the opposite dentate nucleus through the superior cerebellar peduncle, which crosses before reaching it.
That crossing is why each cerebellar hemisphere relates to the same side of the body. (Last's p. 607)
Is slightly larger than a full-sized pea

The red nucleus is slightly larger than a full-sized pea and easy to see in midbrain sections.
Its pink colour in fresh specimens comes from its rich vascularity and iron. (Last's p. 607)
Connects especially with the cortex and globus pallidus

Besides input from the contralateral dentate nucleus, the red nucleus has many connections, especially with the cortex and the globus pallidus.
It gives rise to the rubrospinal tract. (Last's p. 607)
Its efferent fibres decussate at superior colliculus level

Last's places the decussation of the red nucleus efferent fibres at the level of the inferior colliculi, not the superior colliculi.
The red nucleus itself lies at the superior colliculus level; its rubrospinal fibres cross lower down (ventral tegmental decussation). (Last's p. 607)
Is associated with a well-defined human disease

Last's says the red nucleus is not associated with any known disease.
Lesions in its region cause tremor (as in Benedikt's syndrome) because of the dentatothalamic fibres passing through. (Last's p. 607)

questions.s: Midbrain blood supply and related structures:
o: Supplied by the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

The midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries as they curl round the cerebral peduncle, and by perforating branches from the basilar tip.
Their occlusion causes the midbrain syndromes. (Last's p. 607-8)
Veins drain mostly into the basal vein

Midbrain veins drain mostly into the basal vein, and some from the colliculi drain into the great cerebral vein.
Both lead to the straight sinus. (Last's p. 607-8)
The mesencephalic nucleus lies medial to the aqueduct

The mesencephalic nucleus of V lies lateral to the aqueduct in the central grey, not medial.
It extends through the whole length of the midbrain. (Last's p. 607-8)
The medial geniculate body lies at inferior colliculus level

The medial geniculate body lies at the level of the superior colliculus.
It receives from the inferior colliculus through the inferior brachium. (Last's p. 607-8)
The trigeminal is the only nerve to emerge from the pons

V is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the pons itself (its anterolateral surface). Its point of emergence marks the change from pons to middle cerebellar peduncle.
VI, VII and VIII emerge at the pontomedullary junction. (Last's p. 608)
It lies along the clivus separated by the pontine cistern

The ventral surface of the pons lies on the clivus, separated from it by the pontine cistern, which contains the basilar artery.
VI runs up through this cistern. (Last's p. 608)
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery curls round the upper margin of the pons

The superior cerebellar artery curls round the upper margin of the pons. The anterior inferior cerebellar artery runs lower, near the pontomedullary junction.
III and IV pass above the superior cerebellar artery. (Last's p. 608)
The pontine roof of the fourth ventricle is the inferior medullary velum

The roof of the pontine part of the fourth ventricle is the superior medullary velum, with the lingula of the cerebellum on it.
The inferior medullary velum roofs the lower part. (Last's p. 608)
Pontine nuclei send fibres across to form the middle cerebellar peduncle

Pontine nuclei receive corticopontine fibres and send their axons across the midline to form the middle cerebellar peduncle.
This completes the corticopontocerebellar pathway. (Last's p. 608)
The trigeminal motor nucleus lies below the lateral floor of the upper fourth ventricle

The trigeminal motor nucleus lies in the upper pons beneath the lateral part of the floor of the fourth ventricle.
It supplies the first-arch muscles. (Last's p. 608)
The main sensory nucleus lies medial to the motor nucleus

The main sensory nucleus of V lies lateral to the motor nucleus, not medial.
"Motor medial, sensory lateral." (Last's p. 608)
The spinal nucleus subserves touch

The main sensory nucleus subserves touch. The spinal nucleus subserves pain and temperature.
The mesencephalic nucleus subserves proprioception. (Last's p. 608)
The superior salivary nucleus lies alongside the facial nucleus

The superior salivary nucleus lies alongside the facial nucleus in the pons. Its axons leave in the nervus intermedius.
It supplies the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands. (Last's p. 609)
The inferior salivary nucleus lies just above the pontomedullary junction

The inferior salivary nucleus lies just above the pontomedullary junction. Its axons run in IX to the otic ganglion (for the parotid).
It lies caudal to the superior salivary nucleus. (Last's p. 609)
The cochlear nuclei are mainly pontine

Last's says the cochlear nuclei are mainly medullary, not pontine.
They lie on the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the pontomedullary junction. (Last's p. 609)
Vestibular fibres pass posterior to the inferior cerebellar peduncle

Vestibular fibres of VIII pass anterior (ventral) to the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the vestibular nuclei.
The cochlear fibres end on the surface of the peduncle. (Last's p. 609)

questions.s: Pontine blood supply and venous drainage:
o: Mainly pontine branches of the basilar

The pons is supplied mainly by pontine branches of the basilar artery (paramedian and short circumferential).
Basilar occlusion therefore causes extensive pontine infarction. (Last's p. 609)
Contributions from the superior cerebellar and AICA

The superior cerebellar artery and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery also contribute to the supply of the pons, mainly its lateral parts.
These are long circumferential branches. (Last's p. 609)
Venous return is mainly to the superior petrosal sinus

Venous return from the pons is mainly to the inferior petrosal sinuses and the basilar plexus.
The superior petrosal sinus drains more lateral structures. (Last's p. 609)
The pontine reticular formation lies ventral to the pontine nuclei

The pontine reticular formation lies in the tegmentum, dorsal to the pontine nuclei.
The pontine nuclei lie in the basilar (ventral) part. (Last's p. 609)
Lies from a line joining the jugular tubercles to the atlas

The medulla runs nearly vertically from a line joining the jugular tubercles down to the atlas, through the foramen magnum.
Its lower end becomes the spinal cord at C1. (Last's p. 609-10)
It lies in the vallecula of the cerebellum

The medulla sits in the vallecula, the deep groove between the cerebellar hemispheres, behind it.
The tonsils lie on either side, close to the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 609-10)
The closed part is the upper part

The closed part of the medulla is the lower part, containing the central canal. The upper (open) part forms the floor of the fourth ventricle.
The obex marks the junction. (Last's p. 609-10)
The inferior cerebellar peduncle enters above and lateral to the middle peduncle

The inferior cerebellar peduncle enters the cerebellum medial to and below the middle peduncle.
The middle peduncle is the largest and most lateral. (Last's p. 609-10)
The sixth nerve emerges between pons and pyramid

VI emerges at the lower border of the pons, at the junction with the pyramid.
It lies close to the midline, then runs up the clivus. (Last's p. 609-10)
The twelfth emerges between pyramid and olive

XII emerges between the pyramid and the olive, in two small groups of rootlets.
The rootlets unite in the hypoglossal canal. (Last's p. 609-10)
IX, X and cranial XI emerge medial to the olive

IX, X and the cranial XI emerge lateral to (behind) the olive, in the postolivary sulcus.
Only XII emerges in front of the olive. (Last's p. 609-10)
The vagal trigone lies medial to the hypoglossal trigone

The hypoglossal trigone lies next to the midline, with the vagal trigone lateral to it.
Medial to lateral in the lower floor: hypoglossal, vagal, vestibular. (Last's p. 609-10)
The upper medulla shows the sac-like olivary nucleus

A section through the upper medulla is identified by the bulging pyramid and olive and the crenated, sac-like inferior olivary nucleus.
The fourth ventricle forms its dorsal surface. (Last's p. 610)
Pyramidal decussation characterises the lowest part

The visible pyramidal (motor) decussation marks the lowest part of the medulla.
The sensory decussation of the medial lemnisci is at a slightly higher level. (Last's p. 610)
The sensory decussation lies below the pyramidal decussation

The sensory decussation (of the medial lemnisci) lies slightly above the pyramidal decussation, not below.
The motor decussation is the lowest. (Last's p. 610)
The nucleus ambiguus lies superficially beneath the floor of the ventricle

The nucleus ambiguus lies at a deeper level in the reticular formation of the medulla, not just beneath the floor of the ventricle.
Like other branchial motor nuclei, it lies away from the ventricular floor. (Last's p. 610)

questions.s: The nucleus of the tractus solitarius (Last's):
o: Its cells are the most tightly packed of any brainstem nucleus

The cells of the nucleus of the tractus solitarius are the most tightly packed of any brainstem nucleus, surrounding the tract of incoming fibres.
The tract runs through the middle of the nucleus. (Last's p. 610)
The two sides meet in the lowest part of the open medulla

The two nuclei meet in the lowest part of the open medulla, forming a V.
This is the commissural nucleus. (Last's p. 610)
Its lower part receives taste fibres

The upper part of the nucleus receives taste (gustatory nucleus). The lower part receives general visceral afferents.
Taste is rostral. (Last's p. 610)
It contains the expiratory centre

Last's says some of its cells form the inspiratory centre, not the expiratory centre.
The respiratory centres are functional regions rather than discrete nuclei. (Last's p. 610)

questions.s: The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives:
o: Taste fibres from the chorda tympani

Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, carried by the chorda tympani (VII), ends in the upper (gustatory) part of the nucleus.
The cell bodies are in the geniculate ganglion. (Last's p. 610)
Baroreceptor afferents from the carotid sinus

Carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents travel in IX to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
This is the afferent limb of the baroreceptor reflex. (Last's p. 610)
Afferents from the aortic bodies

Chemoreceptor afferents from the aortic bodies travel in X to the nucleus.
Carotid body afferents travel in IX to the same nucleus. (Last's p. 610)
Taste via the internal laryngeal nerve

A few taste fibres from the epiglottis and valleculae travel in the internal laryngeal nerve (X) to the nucleus.
So all three nerves (VII, IX, X) carry taste to this one nucleus. (Last's p. 610)
Its upper part supplies the palate

The nucleus ambiguus is arranged from above down: palate, then pharynx and oesophagus, then larynx. The upper part supplies the palate.
Its fibres leave mainly in X and the cranial accessory. (Last's p. 610-11)
Its lowest part supplies the larynx

The lowest part of the nucleus ambiguus supplies the laryngeal muscles.
So low medullary lesions affect the voice. (Last's p. 610-11)
Its middle part supplies the larynx

The middle part of the nucleus ambiguus supplies the pharynx and oesophagus. The lowest part supplies the larynx.
The order runs palate, pharynx, larynx from above down. (Last's p. 610-11)
All its fibres are distributed by the vagus

Not all its fibres are distributed by the vagus: the fibres to stylopharyngeus run in IX.
The cranial accessory fibres also join the vagus. (Last's p. 610-11)
The spinal trigeminal nucleus lies lateral to the tractus solitarius nucleus

In the medulla the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract lie lateral to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
That lateral position puts them in PICA territory. (Last's p. 610-11)
Olivocerebellar fibres decussate to enter the inferior cerebellar peduncle

Olivocerebellar fibres cross the midline and enter the opposite inferior cerebellar peduncle.
They end as climbing fibres. (Last's p. 610-11)
The accessory cuneate nucleus conveys lower limb proprioception

The accessory cuneate nucleus conveys upper limb proprioception to the cerebellum through cuneocerebellar fibres.
Lower limb proprioception travels through Clarke's column and the dorsal spinocerebellar tract. (Last's p. 610-11)
The gracile and cuneate nuclei give rise to the lateral lemniscus

The gracile and cuneate nuclei give rise to the medial lemniscus. The lateral lemniscus carries auditory fibres.
Medial lemniscus: touch and proprioception; lateral lemniscus: hearing. (Last's p. 610-11)

questions.s: The area postrema and reticular formation (Last's):
o: The area postrema lies medial to each gracile nucleus at the lower angle of the ventricle

The area postrema lies medial to each gracile nucleus at the lower angle of the fourth ventricle.
It is a circumventricular organ. (Last's p. 611)
The area postrema is the chemoreceptor trigger zone

The area postrema is the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vomiting centre, lying outside the blood–brain barrier.
Blood-borne emetic substances act here. (Last's p. 611)
The reticular formation receives cerebellar input from the ipsilateral hemisphere via the dentate

The reticular formation receives cerebellar input from the opposite cerebellar hemisphere.
Cerebellar efferents cross in the superior peduncle. (Last's p. 611)
Spinoreticular fibres are part of the touch pathway

Spinoreticular fibres are part of the pain pathway, concerned with the arousal and emotional aspects of pain.
Touch travels in the dorsal columns and anterior spinothalamic tract. (Last's p. 611)
Results from damage to penetrating branches of the anterior spinal branch of the vertebral

The medial medullary syndrome results from damage to paramedian penetrating branches of the anterior spinal artery (from the vertebral). They supply the pyramid, medial lemniscus and hypoglossal nucleus.
So it is a vertebral or anterior spinal territory syndrome. (Last's p. 611-12)
Causes paralysis of the tongue on the same side

The medial medullary syndrome causes paralysis of the tongue on the same side, from damage to the hypoglossal nucleus or fibres.
The tongue deviates towards the side of the lesion. (Last's p. 611-12)
Causes loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side

It causes hemiplegia and loss of touch and kinaesthetic sense on the opposite side (pyramid and medial lemniscus), not loss of pain and temperature.
Pain and temperature are carried laterally, so they are spared. (Last's p. 611-12)
Causes ipsilateral Horner's syndrome

Horner's syndrome belongs to the lateral medullary syndrome, from damage to the descending sympathetic pathway in the lateral medulla.
The medial syndrome spares it. (Last's p. 611-12)
Ipsilateral vocal fold paralysis from nucleus ambiguus involvement

Damage to the nucleus ambiguus paralyses the ipsilateral palate, pharynx and vocal fold, causing dysphonia and dysphagia.
This is a key feature of the lateral medullary syndrome. (Last's p. 611-12)
Loss of pain and temperature on the same side of the face

Pain and temperature are lost on the same side of the face, because the spinal trigeminal tract carries uncrossed fibres.
The face loss is ipsilateral, the body loss contralateral. (Last's p. 611-12)
Loss of pain and temperature on the same side of the body

Pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side of the body, from the crossed spinothalamic tract (spinal lemniscus).
That gives the classic crossed sensory pattern. (Last's p. 611-12)
Contralateral Horner's syndrome

Horner's syndrome is ipsilateral, from damage to the descending sympathetic pathway on the same side.
These fibres do not cross until they reach the cord. (Last's p. 611-12)

questions.s: Blood supply and venous drainage of the medulla:
o: Ventrally from vertebral and basilar branches

The ventral medulla is supplied by branches of the vertebral and basilar arteries, including the anterior spinal artery.
Occlusion gives the medial medullary syndrome. (Last's p. 611-12)
Laterally and dorsally from PICA

PICA supplies the lateral and dorsal medulla, hence the lateral medullary (PICA) syndrome.
Vertebral artery occlusion can produce the same picture. (Last's p. 611-12)
Veins drain dorsally to the inferior petrosal sinus

Medullary veins drain dorsally to the occipital sinus and ventrally to the basilar plexus and inferior petrosal sinus.
So the inferior petrosal sinus receives the ventral, not dorsal, drainage. (Last's p. 611-12)
Medullary veins do not communicate with spinal veins

Medullary veins communicate with the spinal veins.
This continuity forms a route for venous flow between brain and cord. (Last's p. 611-12)
They arise from cells in layer 5 of MsI

Corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres arise from cells in layer 5 of MsI (primary motor cortex), though only about 40 percent come from this area.
The rest come from widely scattered areas, including premotor and parietal cortex. (Last's p. 612)
About 80% come from the primary motor area

Only about 40 percent of corticospinal fibres come from the primary motor area, not 80 percent.
The rest come from widely scattered cortical areas. (Last's p. 612)
Corticonuclear fibres run in the genu of the internal capsule

Corticonuclear fibres pass through the genu of the internal capsule on their way to the cranial nerve motor nuclei.
They leave the main pathway at the appropriate brainstem levels. (Last's p. 612)
The upper part of the facial nucleus receives only contralateral cortical input

The lower part of the facial nucleus is the important exception, receiving only contralateral cortical input. The upper part receives bilateral input.
Hence forehead sparing in upper motor neurone facial palsy. (Last's p. 612)
Each pyramid contains about one million fibres

Each pyramid contains about one million fibres, of which about 700 000 are small myelinated fibres.
Only a small fraction come from Betz cells. (Last's p. 612)
About 85% of fibres cross in the motor decussation

About 85 percent of pyramidal fibres cross in the motor (pyramidal) decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract. The rest form the anterior corticospinal tract.
The decussation is visible on the surface of the lower medulla. (Last's p. 612)
In the crus, arm fibres lie lateral to leg fibres

In the crus (base of the peduncle) arm fibres lie medial to leg fibres.
The order from medial to lateral is head, arm, trunk, leg. (Last's p. 612)
Anterior corticospinal fibres never cross

Anterior corticospinal fibres eventually cross in the cord, at the segment where they end.
So nearly all corticospinal control is crossed. (Last's p. 612)
Frontopontine fibres occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus

Frontopontine fibres occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus, medial to the corticospinal fibres.
The corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres occupy the middle three-fifths. (Last's p. 612)
Temporo-, parieto- and occipitopontine fibres occupy the lateral one-fifth

Temporo-, parieto- and occipitopontine fibres occupy the lateral one-fifth of the crus.
All corticopontine fibres relay in the pontine nuclei to the cerebellum. (Last's p. 612)
Rubrospinal fibres decussate in the dorsal tegmental decussation

Rubrospinal fibres decussate in the ventral tegmental decussation. Tectospinal fibres cross in the dorsal tegmental decussation.
"Rubro = ventral; tecto = dorsal" (the tectum is dorsal). (Last's p. 612)
The superior cerebellar peduncles decussate at superior colliculus level

The superior cerebellar peduncles decussate at the level of the inferior colliculus.
At the superior colliculus level the red nucleus is seen. (Last's p. 612)
Lies immediately ventral to the periaqueductal grey

The medial longitudinal bundle (fasciculus) lies just ventral to the periaqueductal grey, close to the midline.
It lies next to the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei. (Last's p. 613)
Extends to the upper cervical cord

The medial longitudinal bundle runs from the upper midbrain down to the upper cervical cord, linking the vestibular nuclei with the eye and neck motor nuclei.
It coordinates head and eye movements. (Last's p. 613)
Links mainly the cochlear nuclei with eye-muscle nuclei

The medial longitudinal bundle links mainly the vestibular nuclei (and the abducent internuclear neurons) with III, IV and VI.
Cochlear connections run in the lateral lemniscus. (Last's p. 613)
Lies far lateral to the midline in the medulla

The medial longitudinal bundle stays adjacent to the midline throughout the brainstem.
That is why small midline lesions (for example in multiple sclerosis) can cause bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia. (Last's p. 613)
The lateral reticulospinal tract arises from the medullary reticular formation

The lateral reticulospinal tract arises from the medullary reticular formation and is facilitatory. The medial (anterior) tract is pontine.
Last's notes these opposing roles in muscle tone. (Last's p. 613)
The lateral vestibulospinal tract arises from the lateral vestibular nucleus

The lateral vestibulospinal tract comes from the lateral vestibular nucleus and is important for posture, facilitating extensors.
It descends ipsilaterally to all levels. (Last's p. 613)
The anterior (medial) reticulospinal tract arises from the medulla

The anterior (medial) reticulospinal tract arises from the pontine reticular formation, not the medulla.
The lateral tract is medullary. (Last's p. 613)
The tectospinal tract descends to lumbar levels

The tectospinal tract descends no farther than the cervical cord.
It controls reflex head turning. (Last's p. 613)
Begins in the lower medulla

The medial lemniscus begins in the lower medulla, from the opposite gracile and cuneate nuclei.
It carries touch, vibration and proprioception to the thalamus. (Last's p. 613)
Its fibres cross as internal arcuate fibres

Its fibres cross as internal arcuate fibres in the sensory decussation.
So the medial lemniscus carries information from the opposite side of the body. (Last's p. 613)
Lies laterally in the medulla and moves medially in the midbrain

The medial lemniscus starts adjacent to the midline in the medulla and deviates laterally as it ascends through the pons and midbrain.
In the midbrain it lies lateral, near the surface. (Last's p. 613)
Is joined by the lateral lemniscus

The medial lemniscus is joined by the trigeminal lemniscus (from the face). The lateral lemniscus is auditory.
Together the medial and trigeminal lemnisci reach VPL and VPM. (Last's p. 613)
Most spinal lemniscus fibres end in the reticular formation

Most fibres of the spinal lemniscus (spinothalamic and spinoreticular fibres) end in the reticular formation, so the lemniscus quickly becomes smaller as it ascends.
This reticular input contributes to arousal by pain. (Last's p. 613)
The trapezoid body is formed by decussating cochlear nucleus fibres

The trapezoid body is formed by fibres from the cochlear nuclei decussating at the pontomedullary junction.
They then ascend as the lateral lemniscus. (Last's p. 613)
The posterior spinocerebellar tract enters the superior cerebellar peduncle

The posterior spinocerebellar tract enters the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The anterior tract enters through the superior peduncle.
The anterior tract is the classic exception. (Last's p. 613)
Trigeminal pain fibres synapse before descending in the spinal tract

Trigeminal pain fibres first descend in the spinal tract of V and then synapse in the spinal nucleus.
So a lesion of the spinal tract in the medulla abolishes facial pain even though the fibres entered at the pons. (Last's p. 613)

questions.s: The roof of the fourth ventricle:
o: The superior medullary velum is bounded by the superior cerebellar peduncles

The superior medullary velum is a thin sheet of white matter roofing the pontine part of the fourth ventricle, between the two superior cerebellar peduncles.
IV emerges through it. (Last's p. 613-14)
The inferior medullary velum is white matter from the base of the flocculus

The medullary part of the roof is covered by the inferior medullary velum, a thin sheet of white matter from the base of the flocculus.
Below this the roof is only ependyma and pia (tela choroidea). (Last's p. 613-14)
The median aperture opens into the pontine cistern

The median aperture opens into the cerebellomedullary cistern (cisterna magna).
The lateral apertures open into the pontine cistern. (Last's p. 613-14)
The lateral apertures open posteriorly into the cerebellomedullary cistern

The lateral apertures open anteriorly, just behind VIII, into the pontine cistern.
The median aperture opens posteriorly into the cerebellomedullary cistern. (Last's p. 613-14)

questions.s: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle (Last's):
o: Is supplied by a branch of PICA

The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is supplied by a branch of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.
PICA loops close to the lower part of the ventricle. (Last's p. 613-14)
Lies just below the flocculus at the lateral aperture

The plexus starts at the lateral aperture, just below the flocculus, and can be seen protruding into the cerebellopontine angle.
It is a landmark in cerebellopontine angle surgery. (Last's p. 613-14)
Indents the pontine part of the roof

The choroid plexus indents the medullary part of the roof, not the pontine part.
The pontine part is roofed by the superior medullary velum. (Last's p. 613-14)
Drains to the straight sinus

The fourth ventricle plexus drains to the occipital sinus.
The straight sinus receives the great cerebral vein. (Last's p. 613-14)

questions.s: The floor of the fourth ventricle:
o: The medullary striae are aberrant pontine fibres to the cerebellum

The medullary striae are aberrant fibres from pontine (arcuate) nuclei passing to the cerebellum through the inferior peduncle.
They cross the floor of the ventricle at its widest part. (Last's p. 614)
The locus caeruleus lies in the upper superior fovea

The locus coeruleus lies in the upper part of the floor, at the superior fovea. Its cells are pigmented and noradrenergic.
It gives a bluish colour in fresh specimens. (Last's p. 614)
The facial colliculus lies at the upper end of the medial eminence

The facial colliculus lies at the lower end of the medial eminence (in the pontine part of the floor), not the upper end.
It is just above the medullary striae. (Last's p. 614)
The hypoglossal trigone has its apex upwards

The hypoglossal trigone has its apex downward. The vagal trigone has its apex upward.
The two triangles fit together on either side of the inferior fovea. (Last's p. 614)

questions.s: The medullary part of the floor:
o: Is smaller than the pontine part

The medullary part of the rhomboid fossa (floor of the fourth ventricle) is smaller than the pontine part.
The medullary striae separate them. (Last's p. 614)
The inferior fovea divides it into two triangles

The inferior fovea divides the medullary part of the floor into two triangles: the hypoglossal trigone medially and the vagal trigone laterally.
The vestibular area lies further lateral. (Last's p. 614)
The vagal trigone lies medial to the hypoglossal trigone

The vagal trigone lies lateral to the hypoglossal trigone, not medial.
The somatic motor nucleus (XII) lies nearest the midline. (Last's p. 614)
The vestibular area is confined to the pontine part

The vestibular area extends into the medullary part, its lower part occupying the lateral angle of the medullary floor.
The vestibular nuclei lie in both pons and medulla. (Last's p. 614)
About 30% comes from brain capillaries other than the choroid plexuses

About 30 percent of CSF seeps from brain capillaries via the extracellular fluid, rather than coming from the choroid plexuses.
The plexuses produce the rest. (Last's p. 614)
The total volume is about 130 ml

The total volume of CSF is about 130 ml, at a pressure of about 130 mm of water.
The equality of these numbers makes them easy to remember. (Last's p. 614)
About 75 ml lies in the cranial subarachnoid space

About 75 ml lies in the spinal subarachnoid space and about 25 ml in the cranial subarachnoid space. The remaining 30 ml is in the ventricles.
So most CSF is spinal. (Last's p. 614)
Production is about 150 ml per day

CSF production is over 500 ml per day, not 150 ml.
So the whole volume is replaced about four times a day. (Last's p. 614)
About 30 ml is within the ventricular system

Only about 30 ml of CSF is within the ventricular system. About 100 ml is in the subarachnoid space (75 ml of it spinal).
So a large proportion surrounds the cord. (Last's p. 614)
Some drains through the cribriform plate to cervical lymphatics

Besides the arachnoid granulations, some CSF drains through the cribriform plate into the nasal tissues and cervical lymphatics.
This lymphatic route is increasingly recognised. (Last's p. 614)
CSF pressure follows arterial pressure closely

Arterial pressure changes have little effect on CSF pressure, whereas venous pressure changes are quickly reflected.
That is why coughing, straining or jugular compression raise CSF pressure. (Last's p. 614)
Buoyancy reduces the brain's effective weight to about 500 g

Buoyancy reduces the brain's effective weight from about 1500 g to about 50 g, not 500 g.
This protects the brain from its own weight. (Last's p. 614)
Sensory nuclei contain cell bodies of second neurons

The sensory nuclei of the cranial nerves contain the cell bodies of second-order neurons. The first neurons lie in the sensory ganglia.
The mesencephalic nucleus of V is the exception. (Last's p. 614-15)
The trigeminal motor nucleus supplies mylohyoid and tensor palati

The trigeminal motor nucleus supplies the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, the anterior belly of digastric, tensor palati and tensor tympani.
These are all first-arch derivatives. (Last's p. 614-15)
The oculomotor somatic nucleus is level with the inferior colliculi

The somatic oculomotor nucleus is level with the superior colliculi. The trochlear nucleus is at the level of the inferior colliculi.
"Three is superior, four is inferior." (Last's p. 614-15)
The main sensory trigeminal nucleus lies medial to the motor nucleus

The main sensory trigeminal nucleus lies lateral to the motor nucleus, not medial.
This is the usual pattern: motor medial, sensory lateral. (Last's p. 614-15)
The nucleus ambiguus lies deep in the upper medulla

The nucleus ambiguus lies deep in the upper medulla. It is the branchial motor nucleus of IX, X and the cranial accessory.
It supplies the palate, pharynx, larynx and upper oesophagus. (Last's p. 615-16)
IX carries carotid body chemoreceptor fibres to the tractus solitarius

The carotid sinus nerve of IX carries carotid body chemoreceptor fibres (and sinus baroreceptor fibres) to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
It is the afferent limb of the reflexes controlling breathing and blood pressure. (Last's p. 615-16)
X carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue

IX carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue. X carries taste from the epiglottis region.
VII covers the anterior two-thirds. (Last's p. 615-16)
The tractus solitarius lies medial to the dorsal vagal nucleus

The nucleus of the tractus solitarius lies lateral to the dorsal vagal nucleus.
In the floor: hypoglossal medial, dorsal vagal intermediate, solitarius and vestibular lateral. (Last's p. 615-16)

questions.s: Brainstem death tests and their anatomical basis (Last's):
o: Fixed pupils test midbrain function

Pupils fixed to light indicate loss of the midbrain light reflex pathway (pretectum and Edinger–Westphal nuclei, with III).
This is one of the brainstem death tests. (Last's p. 616)
Absent corneal reflex tests pontine trigeminal-facial connections

The corneal reflex uses trigeminal afferents and facial efferents connected in the pons. Its absence indicates loss of pontine function.
Both sides are tested. (Last's p. 616)
Absent gag reflex tests pontine connexions

The gag reflex tests the glossopharyngeal and vagal connexions in the medulla, not the pons.
The cough reflex (vagal) tests the medulla too. (Last's p. 616)
The apnoea test requires PaCO2 above 30 mm Hg

The apnoea test requires the PaCO2 to rise above 50 mm Hg (6.7 kPa) without any respiratory effort.
30 mm Hg would be too low to stimulate breathing reliably. (Last's p. 616)
The superior peduncle enters the midbrain

The superior cerebellar peduncle enters the midbrain, the middle peduncle enters the pons and the inferior peduncle enters the medulla.
Each peduncle links to a different part of the brainstem. (Last's p. 616)
The archaeocerebellum is concerned with balance

The archaeocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is concerned with balance and vestibular mechanisms.
Its lesions cause truncal ataxia. (Last's p. 616)
The palaeocerebellum is associated with the cerebral hemispheres

The palaeocerebellum is associated with spinal mechanisms (limb movements and posture). The neocerebellum is associated with the cerebral hemispheres.
Archaeo = vestibular; palaeo = spinal; neo = cerebral. (Last's p. 616)
The highest part of the cerebellum lies at the attached margin of the tentorium

The highest part of the cerebellum lies at the tentorial notch, not at the attached margin of the tentorium.
The tentorium slopes down from the notch to its attached margin. (Last's p. 616)
The horizontal fissure is the deepest sulcus

The horizontal fissure is the deepest sulcus of the cerebellum, but Last's says it has no functional significance.
It runs around the lateral and posterior margin. (Last's p. 617)
The primary fissure separates palaeocerebellum from neocerebellum

The primary fissure on the superior surface separates the anterior lobe (palaeocerebellum) from the posterior lobe (neocerebellum).
It is the functionally important fissure. (Last's p. 617)
The anterior lobe is large and the posterior lobe small

The anterior lobe is small and the posterior lobe large.
The neocerebellum (posterior lobe) expanded greatly in humans. (Last's p. 617)
The primary fissure lies on the inferior surface

The primary fissure lies on the superior surface, in front of the horizontal fissure.
The posterolateral fissure lies on the inferior surface. (Last's p. 617)
The inferior vermis consists of pyramid, uvula and nodule

In the vallecula the inferior vermis consists of three lobules: pyramid, uvula and nodule.
They lie between the cerebellar hemispheres on the under surface. (Last's p. 617)
The nodule lies highest, on the roof of the fourth ventricle

The nodule is the highest lobule of the inferior vermis, lying on the roof of the fourth ventricle and joined laterally to the flocculi.
Together they form the flocculonodular lobe. (Last's p. 617)
The flocculonodular lobe and pyramid form the archaeocerebellum

Last's says the archaeocerebellum consists of the flocculonodular lobe and the lingula, not the pyramid.
The pyramid belongs to the palaeocerebellum. (Last's p. 617)
The paraflocculus lies above the flocculus

The paraflocculus lies beneath the flocculus, attached mainly to the pyramid.
It is small in humans. (Last's p. 617)
Archaeocerebellar lesions cause trunk ataxia

Archaeocerebellar lesions cause truncal ataxia, without nystagmus or tremor according to Last's.
The patient cannot sit or stand steadily. (Last's p. 617-18)
Neocerebellar lesions cause intention tremor

Neocerebellar lesions cause intention tremor, hypotonia, pendular jerks, dysdiadochokinesia and nystagmus.
These are the typical "cerebellar hemisphere" signs on the same side. (Last's p. 617-18)
Palaeocerebellar lesions cause reduced muscle reflexes

Last's says palaeocerebellar lesions cause increased muscle reflexes with disturbed postural mechanisms.
Hypotonia and pendular reflexes are neocerebellar features. (Last's p. 617-18)
Cerebellar lesions cause paralysis

Cerebellar lesions do not cause paralysis.
They disturb coordination and tone, not strength. (Last's p. 617-18)
The dentate opens towards the superior peduncle

The crenated dentate nucleus opens medially towards the superior cerebellar peduncle, through which its efferent fibres leave.
Its shape resembles the inferior olivary nucleus. (Last's p. 618)
From lateral to medial: emboliform, globose, fastigial

From lateral to medial, the smaller deep nuclei are emboliform, globose and fastigial (with the dentate most lateral of all).
A memory aid: "Don't Eat Greasy Food" (lateral to medial). (Last's p. 618)
The fastigial nucleus belongs to the palaeocerebellum

The fastigial nucleus belongs to the archaeocerebellum (vestibular), connecting with the vestibular nuclei.
The globose and emboliform are palaeocerebellar; the dentate is neocerebellar. (Last's p. 618)
Dentate efferents go to the ipsilateral red nucleus

Dentate efferents go to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus, crossing in the decussation of the superior peduncles.
That is why cerebellar control is ipsilateral overall: the pathway crosses twice. (Last's p. 618)
The molecular layer is superficial

The molecular layer is the superficial layer of the cerebellar cortex, made mostly of fibres (parallel fibres and Purkinje dendrites) with few cells.
It contains basket and stellate cells. (Last's p. 618)
Purkinje cells lie between molecular and granular layers

A single layer of large Purkinje cells lies between the superficial molecular layer and the deep granular layer.
Their axons are the only output of the cortex. (Last's p. 618)
Climbing fibres act through granule cells

Climbing fibres activate Purkinje cells directly. Mossy fibres act indirectly through granule cells (and basket cells).
Climbing fibres come from the inferior olive. (Last's p. 618)
Purkinje dendrites lie parallel to the long axis of a folium

Purkinje cell dendrites spread in a plane at right angles to the long axis of the folium.
Parallel fibres run along the folium, crossing many dendritic trees. (Last's p. 618)
A climbing fibre activates one Purkinje cell

Each climbing fibre wraps around the dendrites of a single Purkinje cell and activates it directly and powerfully.
By contrast, a mossy fibre indirectly influences many hundreds of Purkinje cells through granule cells. (Last's p. 618-19)
A basket cell axon arborises around some 500 Purkinje cells

Each basket cell axon divides and arborises around the cell bodies of some 500 Purkinje cells, inhibiting them.
Basket cells are activated by the parallel fibres of granule cells. (Last's p. 618-19)
A mossy fibre directly activates a single Purkinje cell

Last's says a mossy fibre activates Purkinje cells indirectly, through granule (and basket) cells, and so influences many hundreds of them. It is the climbing fibre that directly activates one Purkinje cell.
Note on sources: Last's text calls climbing fibres the terminals of pontine and vestibular fibres, but standard anatomy (and this bank elsewhere) says climbing fibres come from the inferior olive and mossy fibres from pontine, vestibular and spinal sources. Use the standard version. (Last's p. 618-19)
Efferent fibres generally arise from the cortex

Last's general rule is that efferent fibres of the cerebellum arise from the subcortical (deep) nuclei, not from the cortex. Incoming fibres go to the cortex.
A few cerebellovestibular fibres from the cortex are the clinically unimportant exception. (Last's p. 618-19)
The superior peduncle is predominantly efferent

The superior cerebellar peduncle carries mainly efferent fibres, from the dentate to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. It also carries the afferent anterior spinocerebellar tract.
It is the main output pathway of the cerebellum. (Last's p. 619)
The middle peduncle carries fibres from contralateral pontine nuclei

The middle cerebellar peduncle consists of pontocerebellar fibres from the opposite pontine nuclei, afferent to the neocerebellum.
It is the largest peduncle. (Last's p. 619)
The anterior spinocerebellar tract runs in the inferior peduncle

The anterior spinocerebellar tract runs in the superior peduncle. The posterior spinocerebellar tract runs in the inferior peduncle.
The anterior tract is the exception among cerebellar afferents. (Last's p. 619)
Olivocerebellar fibres come from the ipsilateral olive

Olivocerebellar fibres come from the opposite inferior olive, crossing the midline before entering the inferior peduncle.
So each cerebellar hemisphere receives from the opposite olive. (Last's p. 619)
PICA is the largest branch of the vertebral artery

PICA is the largest branch of the vertebral artery and one of the most tortuous arteries in the body.
Its loops can extend down below the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 619)
PICA passes between the rootlets of IX and X

PICA passes below the hypoglossal rootlets, then between the rootlets of IX and X (or X and XI), as it winds around the medulla.
These relations matter in surgery at the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 619)
AICA arises from the basilar at the upper part of the pons

AICA arises from the basilar artery at the lower part of the pons, not the upper part.
The superior cerebellar artery arises at the upper part, just below the basilar bifurcation. (Last's p. 619)
The superior cerebellar artery winds round the peduncle above the fourth nerve

The superior cerebellar artery winds round the cerebral peduncle below IV (and below III).
The nerves lie above it, between it and the posterior cerebral artery. (Last's p. 619)
Superior and posterior surfaces drain to straight and transverse sinuses

Cerebellar veins drain to the nearest sinus: the superior and posterior surfaces drain to the straight and transverse sinuses.
There are no deep veins draining the cerebellum centrally. (Last's p. 619)
The superior vermis drains to the great cerebral vein

The superior vermis drains to the great cerebral vein at its entrance to the straight sinus.
So superior vermian veins join the deep venous system. (Last's p. 619)
The inferior surfaces drain to the superior petrosal sinus

The inferior surfaces drain to the inferior petrosal, sigmoid and occipital sinuses, not the superior petrosal sinus.
The superior petrosal sinus drains the anterior (petrosal) surface. (Last's p. 619)
Two arteries supply the small upper surface of each hemisphere

Last's says one artery (the superior cerebellar) supplies the small upper surface of each hemisphere, and two (AICA and PICA) supply the large under surface.
The upper surface is smaller. (Last's p. 619)
In the fetus it reaches S2 vertebra

In the fetus the spinal cord fills the dural sac down to the level of S2. The vertebral column and dura then outgrow it.
So the cord "ascends" relative to the column. (Last's p. 619-20)
At birth the conus lies opposite L3

At birth the conus medullaris lies opposite L3.
It reaches its adult level (L1–2) later. (Last's p. 619-20)
It reaches its adult level at about 5 years

The cord reaches its adult level at about 20 years, not 5.
Lumbar puncture in infants must be done lower (L4/5 or below). (Last's p. 619-20)
The cervical enlargement occupies segments C3 to T1

The cervical enlargement occupies cord segments C5 to T1 (for the brachial plexus), at vertebral levels C3 to T1.
C3 is the vertebral level, not the segment. (Last's p. 619-20)
The lumbosacral enlargement spans segments L2 to S3

The lumbosacral enlargement occupies cord segments L2 to S3, supplying the lumbar and sacral plexuses.
It tapers into the conus. (Last's p. 619-20)
It lies opposite vertebrae T9 to L1

Because the cord is shorter than the column, segments L2 to S3 lie opposite vertebrae T9 to L1.
So a T12 vertebral fracture can damage lumbar and sacral segments. (Last's p. 619-20)
Each anterior root has ten or more rootlets

Each anterior root is formed by three or four rootlets, not ten or more.
Posterior roots have more rootlets. (Last's p. 619-20)
The roots unite inside the dural theca

The anterior and posterior roots evaginate the dura separately and unite in the intervertebral foramina, beyond the ganglion.
They do not unite inside the dural theca. (Last's p. 619-20)
Cervical posterior root ganglia lie just lateral to the foramina

Cervical posterior root ganglia lie just lateral to the intervertebral foramina, in contact with the vertebral artery.
Lower down the ganglia lie within the foramina. (Last's p. 620)
The cauda equina consists of nerve roots, not nerves

Below L1 the roots descend in the subarachnoid space as the cauda equina. Spinal nerves form only at the foramina, so the cauda consists of roots, not nerves.
That is why the cauda behaves differently from cord or peripheral nerve lesions. (Last's p. 620)
The filum terminale is part of the cauda equina

The filum terminale is pia mater and is not classified as part of the cauda equina, though it runs among its roots.
The cauda consists only of nerve roots. (Last's p. 620)
Upper thoracic roots kink downwards to reach their foramina

Upper thoracic roots kink upward to reach their foramina, because the posterior root ganglia are fixed in the foramina at a higher level.
Lower roots run increasingly obliquely downward. (Last's p. 620)
The central canal extends into the upper few mm of the filum

The central canal continues into the top few millimetres of the filum terminale.
It may be dilated in the conus as the terminal ventricle. (Last's p. 620)
The white commissure lies anterior to the grey commissure

A narrow white commissure lies in front of the grey commissure, at the depth of the anterior median fissure.
Spinothalamic fibres cross in it, so central cord lesions affect them first. (Last's p. 620)
Posterior white columns are largest in the lumbar region

The posterior white columns are largest in the cervical region, because fibres from all lower levels have been added.
In the lumbar region they are smallest. (Last's p. 620)
The anterior horn reaches the surface of the cord

The anterior horn falls short of the surface of the cord. The posterior horn reaches the surface.
The dorsolateral (Lissauer's) tract caps the posterior horn. (Last's p. 620)
Medial cells supply trunk muscles

Medial anterior horn cells supply the trunk muscles, which is why they are present at every level of the cord.
They form a constant medial column. (Last's p. 621-2)
Lateral cells supply limbs

Lateral anterior horn cells supply the limbs and make up the cervical and lumbosacral enlargements.
They are absent from most thoracic segments. (Last's p. 621-2)
Dorsal cells of the lateral group supply proximal limb muscles

Within the lateral group, ventral cells supply proximal limb muscles and dorsal cells supply distal limb muscles.
"Proximal anterior, distal posterior"; flexors are dorsal to extensors. (Last's p. 621-2)
The sympathetic lateral horn spans T1 to L4

The sympathetic lateral horn spans T1 to L2, not T1 to L4.
This is the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow. (Last's p. 621-2)
Lamina II is the gelatinous substance

Lamina II is the substantia gelatinosa, where pain fibres arriving from Lissauer's tract synapse.
It is a key site of pain modulation (gate control). (Last's p. 621-2)
The thoracic nucleus is in the medial part of lamina VII

The thoracic nucleus (Clarke's column) lies in the medial part of lamina VII at the base of the posterior horn.
It gives rise to the posterior spinocerebellar tract. (Last's p. 621-2)
Laminae VII and VIII form the nucleus proprius

The nucleus proprius is formed by laminae III to VI. Laminae VII and VIII are intermediate and ventral grey.
Lamina IX contains the motor neurons. (Last's p. 621-2)
Lamina V contains the alpha motor neurons

The alpha motor neurons lie in lamina IX. Lamina V is a main source of anterolateral (spinothalamic) tract fibres.
Laminae I and V are the main pain projection laminae. (Last's p. 621-2)
Anterior roots divide lateral from anterior white columns

The emerging anterior roots form the dividing line between the lateral and anterior white columns.
The posterior roots divide the posterior and lateral columns. (Last's p. 622-3)
Propriospinal fibres lie adjacent to the grey matter

Short intersegmental (propriospinal) fibres run next to the grey matter, linking cord segments.
They allow coordination between segments. (Last's p. 622-3)
Tracts have sharp boundaries throughout the cord

Except in the posterior columns, the tracts of the spinal cord have no sharp boundaries; they overlap.
So tract diagrams are only approximations. (Last's p. 622-3)
The posterior column contains descending fibres

The posterior column is wholly occupied by ascending gracile and cuneate fibres (with their collaterals).
Descending tracts lie in the lateral and anterior columns. (Last's p. 622-3)
Fibres from the lowest segments lie nearest the midline

The posterior columns are laminated: sacral and lumbar fibres lie nearest the midline in the gracile tract, and upper limb fibres lie laterally in the cuneate tract.
Each new set of fibres is added laterally. (Last's p. 622-3)
They carry the sense of bladder and rectal fullness

Besides touch, vibration and position sense, the posterior columns carry the sense of bladder and rectal fullness.
So posterior column lesions can affect awareness of bladder filling. (Last's p. 622-3)
Fibres enter on the lateral side of the posterior roots

Fibres destined for the posterior columns enter on the medial side of the posterior root.
The finer pain fibres enter laterally, into Lissauer's tract. (Last's p. 622-3)
The gracile tract carries upper limb fibres

The gracile tract carries fibres from the lower trunk, lower limb and perineum. The cuneate tract carries the upper limb.
Gracile = leg (medial); cuneate = arm (lateral). (Last's p. 622-3)
Romberg's sign indicates sensory ataxia

Romberg's sign indicates sensory ataxia: with loss of position sense the patient sways or falls when the eyes are closed.
Vision compensates when the eyes are open. (Last's p. 623-4)
Two points 3 mm apart are normally distinguishable on the finger pads

Two points about 3 mm apart are normally distinguishable on the finger pads. This needs intact posterior column pathways and cortex.
The distance is much larger on the back. (Last's p. 623-4)
Vibration is tested with a 512 Hz fork

Last's says vibration is tested with a 128 Hz tuning fork.
The 512 Hz fork is used for hearing tests (Rinne and Weber). (Last's p. 623-4)
Cerebellar ataxia worsens markedly with eyes closed

With cerebellar or labyrinthine ataxia there is little difference between eyes open and closed.
Marked worsening with the eyes closed points to sensory ataxia. (Last's p. 623-4)
Lies in front of the lateral corticospinal tract

The anterolateral tract lies in front of the lateral corticospinal tract and in front of the denticulate ligament.
That is why cordotomy cuts are made in front of the ligament. (Last's p. 623-4)
Arises mainly from laminae I and V

Most anterolateral tract fibres arise from second-order cells in laminae I and V.
These cells receive nociceptive input. (Last's p. 623-4)
Fibres cross behind the central canal

Anterolateral fibres cross in front of the central canal, in the anterior white commissure.
So a central cord lesion (syringomyelia) cuts them first. (Last's p. 623-4)
Cervical fibres lie most laterally

In the anterolateral tract sacral fibres lie most laterally (superficially) and cervical fibres most deeply.
That explains sacral sparing with central cord lesions. (Last's p. 623-4)
C fibres carry slow pain

Unmyelinated C fibres carry slow, burning, poorly localised pain.
They end mainly in laminae I and II. (Last's p. 623-4)
A-delta fibres carry fast pain and temperature

Thinly myelinated A-delta fibres carry fast, sharp pain and temperature.
They give the first, well-localised pain after an injury. (Last's p. 623-4)
Lissauer's tract fibres run 5-6 segments before synapsing

Lissauer's tract fibres run only one or two segments before synapsing, not five or six.
So the sensory level of a cord lesion lies close to the lesion. (Last's p. 623-4)
Crude touch fibres occupy the lateral part of the tract

Crude touch fibres occupy the more medial part of the anterolateral tract and cross less obliquely.
Pain and temperature fibres lie more laterally. (Last's p. 623-4)
About 10% of anterolateral fibres pass directly to the thalamus

Only about 10 percent of anterolateral tract fibres pass directly to the thalamus in the spinal lemniscus.
The direct path gives localisation of pain. (Last's p. 624)
The rest synapse in the reticular formation

The other 90 percent synapse in the reticular formation (spinoreticulothalamic path).
This indirect path gives the arousal and unpleasantness of pain. (Last's p. 624)
Endogenous opioid peptides readily cross the blood-brain barrier

Endogenous opioid peptides do not readily cross the blood–brain barrier.
They act locally within the CNS. (Last's p. 624)
Deep pain is tested by pinprick

Pinprick tests superficial pain. Deep pain is tested by squeezing muscles or tendons.
Both should be tested in a full examination. (Last's p. 624)
The knife enters in front of the denticulate ligament

In anterolateral cordotomy the knife enters in front of the denticulate ligament, to spare the lateral corticospinal tract, which lies behind it.
The ligament is the surgeon's landmark. (Last's p. 625)
The cut is made several segments above the desired level

The cut is made several segments above the desired level of analgesia, because pain fibres cross obliquely over several segments before joining the tract.
Otherwise the top of the painful area would be missed. (Last's p. 625)
Pain relief is usually permanent

Last's says pain relief after cordotomy rarely lasts more than a few months (two years at most).
Alternative pathways take over. (Last's p. 625)
It divides the medial part of the anterolateral tract

Cordotomy divides the lateral (superficial) part of the anterolateral tract, which carries pain and temperature.
The medial part carries crude touch. (Last's p. 625)
Clarke's column spans all thoracic and first two lumbar segments

Clarke's column (thoracic nucleus) runs from T1 to L2. It does not extend above T1, so cervical proprioception reaches the cerebellum by the cuneocerebellar route instead.
Lower lumbar and sacral fibres ascend in the gracile tract to reach it. (Last's p. 625)
The posterior spinocerebellar tract is uncrossed

The posterior spinocerebellar tract is uncrossed and enters the cerebellum through the inferior peduncle.
So it carries ipsilateral unconscious proprioception. (Last's p. 625)
The anterior spinocerebellar tract is mostly uncrossed

The anterior spinocerebellar tract mostly crosses in the cord, then crosses back in the cerebellum, entering through the superior peduncle.
The net effect is still ipsilateral cerebellar representation. (Last's p. 625)
Cervical proprioception travels in the posterior spinocerebellar tract

Cervical proprioception travels via the accessory cuneate nucleus and the cuneocerebellar tract.
The posterior spinocerebellar tract starts at T1. (Last's p. 625)
Lies behind the attachment of the denticulate ligament

The lateral corticospinal tract lies behind the attachment of the denticulate ligament, which is why cordotomy is done in front of the ligament.
It occupies the posterior part of the lateral column. (Last's p. 625)
Arm fibres cross slightly higher than leg fibres

In the pyramidal decussation, arm fibres cross slightly higher than leg fibres.
This explains some unusual patterns of weakness with lesions at the decussation (cruciate paralysis). (Last's p. 625)
About 25% of fibres supply the upper limb

About 55 percent of corticospinal fibres end at cervical and T1 levels (for the upper limb); about 25 percent supply the lower limb.
The hand is heavily represented. (Last's p. 625)
Most fibres synapse directly on motor neurons

About 98 percent of corticospinal fibres synapse with interneurons in laminae VII and VIII, not directly on motor neurons.
Direct connections are mainly to the motor neurons of the hand. (Last's p. 625)
The lateral reticulospinal tract is facilitatory

The lateral (medullary) reticulospinal tract is facilitatory to anterior horn cells.
It increases muscle tone. (Last's p. 625)
The medial reticulospinal tract is inhibitory

The medial (pontine) reticulospinal tract is inhibitory, according to Last's.
The balance between the two helps set muscle tone. (Last's p. 625)
The anterior corticospinal tract reaches the sacral cord

The anterior corticospinal tract reaches no lower than the upper thoracic cord.
It mainly controls neck and trunk muscles. (Last's p. 625)
The vestibulospinal tract mainly affects distal limb muscles

The vestibulospinal tract mainly affects trunk and limb girdle muscles, for posture.
Distal limb muscles are controlled mainly by the corticospinal tract. (Last's p. 625)
A pure pyramidal lesion causes flaccid paralysis

Last's says a lesion confined to the medullary pyramid gives flaccid, not spastic, paralysis.
Pure pyramidal tract lesions are rare. (Last's p. 625-6)
Spasticity reflects concomitant extrapyramidal involvement

Spasticity in the usual upper motor neurone lesion is due to extrapyramidal fibres being damaged as well, releasing anterior horn cells from inhibition.
Pure pyramidal fibres are not responsible for the spasticity. (Last's p. 625-6)
A pure pyramidal lesion can arise in the internal capsule

Last's says a pure pyramidal lesion is possible from a lesion confined to the medullary pyramid. In the internal capsule the pyramidal and extrapyramidal fibres are mixed, so lesions there are not pure.
That is why capsular strokes cause spasticity. (Last's p. 625-6)
Parasagittal meningioma affects both arm areas

A parasagittal meningioma presses on the leg areas of both hemispheres, which lie next to the falx.
It may cause a spastic paraparesis mimicking a cord lesion. (Last's p. 625-6)
The anterior spinal artery forms from both vertebral arteries

The anterior spinal artery forms at the foramen magnum from a branch of each vertebral artery.
It runs down the anterior median fissure. (Last's p. 626)
It supplies the cord anterior to the posterior grey columns

The anterior spinal artery supplies everything in front of the posterior grey columns, on both sides.
So its occlusion spares the posterior columns. (Last's p. 626)
The posterior spinal arteries arise from the anterior spinal artery

The posterior spinal arteries arise from PICA or the vertebral artery, not from the anterior spinal artery.
They are usually double on each side. (Last's p. 626)
The anterior spinal artery is largest in the thoracic region

The anterior spinal artery may become so small in the thoracic region that it is considered absent.
That makes the thoracic cord a watershed zone vulnerable to ischaemia. (Last's p. 626)
Embryonically every segment has a radicular vessel on both sides

In the embryo every segment has a radicular artery on both sides. Most regress, leaving a variable few feeders to the cord.
The number and position of the survivors varies widely. (Last's p. 626)
Adamkiewicz is slightly commoner on the left

The arteria radicularis magna (of Adamkiewicz) is slightly commoner on the left, though it may be anywhere from T7 to L4.
It is the main supply of the lower cord. (Last's p. 626)
Adamkiewicz always accompanies T10 or T11

Adamkiewicz may enter anywhere from T7 to L4, so it does not always accompany T10 or T11.
Surgeons cannot rely on its position without imaging. (Last's p. 626)
Lateral sacral arteries never give radicular branches

The lateral sacral arteries are among the parent vessels that give radicular branches.
Radicular arteries also arise from vertebral, ascending cervical, intercostal and lumbar arteries. (Last's p. 626)
Pial arteries supply the periphery of the cord

A pial plexus fed by the anterior, posterior and radicular arteries supplies the periphery of the cord.
Central branches supply the deeper parts. (Last's p. 626)
Sacral sparing results from pial supply to superficial sacral fibres

Sacral fibres are most superficial in the long tracts and keep a pial supply, so anterior spinal artery occlusion may spare them (sacral sparing).
Sacral sparing is an important sign of an incomplete lesion. (Last's p. 626)
Posterior spinal veins are single

The posterior spinal veins are double, straddling the posterior roots.
The anterior spinal vein is single. (Last's p. 626)
Spinal veins drain to the azygos system in the lumbar region

In the lumbar region spinal veins drain to lumbar veins. They drain to the azygos system in the thorax.
The vertebral venous plexus links them all. (Last's p. 626)
Transection above T10 abolishes effective cough

Transection of the cord above T10 abolishes an effective cough because the abdominal and lower intercostal muscles are paralysed.
These muscles generate the force of coughing. (Last's p. 627)
Perianal sensation tests conduction through the cord

Preserved perianal sensation and anal reflex show that conduction continues through the whole cord, meaning the lesion is incomplete.
This carries a much better prognosis. (Last's p. 627)
Brown-Sequard causes ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature

In Brown-Séquard syndrome pain and temperature are lost on the opposite (contralateral) side below the lesion.
Motor loss and posterior column loss are ipsilateral. (Last's p. 627)
In anterior spinal artery syndrome touch is lost

In anterior spinal artery syndrome the posterior columns are spared, so touch, vibration and position sense remain intact.
Pain and temperature and motor function are lost. (Last's p. 627)
Commonly follows sudden hyperextension of the cervical spine

Central cord syndrome typically follows sudden hyperextension of the cervical spine, often in a stenotic or spondylotic spine.
The arms are affected more than the legs. (Last's p. 627)
Causes flaccid upper limb paralysis

Damage to the anterior horn cells at the injured segments causes flaccid (lower motor neurone) paralysis in the upper limbs.
The lesion is centred on the grey matter. (Last's p. 627)
Lower limb spasticity arises from sacral corticospinal fibres

Lower limb spasticity arises from damage to the lumbar corticospinal fibres. Sacral fibres lie more superficially and are often spared.
So bladder and bowel may be relatively preserved. (Last's p. 627)
It spares upper limb pain sensation

Central cord syndrome interrupts the deep cervical anterolateral fibres crossing near the central canal, so upper limb pain sensation is affected.
A cape-like distribution of sensory loss is typical of central lesions. (Last's p. 627)

questions.s: The sulcus limitans and nuclear columns (Last's):
o: The alar lamina is dorsal and sensory

The sulcus limitans divides the dorsal alar lamina (sensory) from the ventral basal lamina (motor).
This plan persists from cord to brainstem. (Last's p. 627)
Autonomic cells lie near the sulcus limitans

In each lamina, visceral (autonomic) cells lie next to the sulcus limitans and somatic cells further away.
So visceral motor and visceral sensory columns lie side by side. (Last's p. 627)
Somatic cells lie nearest the sulcus limitans

Somatic cells lie further away from the sulcus limitans. Visceral cells lie nearest it.
In the brainstem floor, somatic motor nuclei (XII) are medial, visceral nuclei intermediate. (Last's p. 627)
In the fourth ventricle efferent cells lie lateral

In the floor of the fourth ventricle, efferent (motor) cells lie medial and afferent (sensory) cells lateral.
The ventricle opening out turned "ventral" into "medial". (Last's p. 627)
Somatic motor nuclei lie near the midline

The somatic motor nuclei (III, IV, VI and XII) lie near the midline.
They supply muscles derived from somites. (Last's p. 627-8)
The branchial column is sometimes called special visceral

The branchial motor column (trigeminal motor, facial and nucleus ambiguus) is sometimes called special visceral efferent; Last's prefers "branchial".
It supplies pharyngeal arch muscles. (Last's p. 627-8)
The nucleus ambiguus has migrated medially

The nucleus ambiguus has migrated laterally (and deep), away from the ventricular floor.
Branchial motor nuclei all lie in this displaced position. (Last's p. 627-8)
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus has migrated laterally

The Edinger–Westphal nucleus has migrated medially, lying cranial (and dorsal) to the somatic oculomotor nucleus.
It is a visceral motor nucleus. (Last's p. 627-8)
From medial to lateral: visceral, branchial, somatic

The afferent columns of the brainstem lie from medial to lateral as visceral, branchial (special visceral) and somatic, the reverse of the motor columns.
So the general somatic afferent (trigeminal) column is lateral. (Last's p. 628-9)
Cochlear and vestibular nuclei form a special somatic group lying farthest laterally

The cochlear and vestibular nuclei form a special somatic afferent column that lies farthest laterally, with no counterpart in the spinal cord.
They develop from the rhombic lip. (Last's p. 628-9)
Each afferent column consists of several separate nuclei

Last's says each afferent column consists of a single nuclear mass, not several separate nuclei.
For example the nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives VII, IX and X. (Last's p. 628-9)
The dorsal nucleus of the vagus is currently regarded as mixed motor and sensory

Recent authorities regard the dorsal nucleus of the vagus as purely motor (parasympathetic).
Visceral sensory fibres of X go to the tractus solitarius instead. (Last's p. 628-9)

questions.s: The posterior parts of the internal capsule (Last's):
o: Thalamocortical fibres lie beside and behind corticospinal fibres

In the posterior limb, thalamocortical sensory fibres lie beside and behind the corticospinal fibres.
A posterior lesion can therefore cause hemianaesthesia. (Last's p. 584-5)
The retrolentiform part carries the optic radiation

The retrolentiform part carries the optic radiation from the lateral geniculate body.
It lies behind the lentiform nucleus. (Last's p. 584-5)
The sublentiform part carries the optic radiation

The sublentiform part carries the auditory radiation. The optic radiation is retrolentiform.
"Auditory below, visual behind." (Last's p. 584-5)
Parieto-, occipito- and temporopontine fibres occupy the medial third of the peduncle base

Parieto-, occipito- and temporopontine fibres occupy the lateral third (fifth) of the base of the peduncle. The frontopontine fibres are medial.
Corticospinal fibres are in the middle. (Last's p. 584-5)

questions.s: The floor of the third ventricle (Last's):
o: The median eminence lies at the base of the infundibulum

The median eminence lies at the base of the infundibulum and is part of the tuber cinereum.
It is where releasing hormones enter the portal vessels. (Last's p. 594)
The supraoptic recess lies between lamina terminalis and chiasma

The small supraoptic recess lies in the angle between the lamina terminalis and the optic chiasma.
The infundibular recess lies behind the chiasma. (Last's p. 594)
The mamillary bodies indent the inside of the ventricle

Last's says the mammillary bodies make no mark on the inside of the third ventricle.
They are seen only on the external surface of the base of the brain. (Last's p. 594)
The anterior commissure is a commissure of the neopallium

The anterior commissure is a commissure of the archaeopallium (olfactory and temporal regions). The corpus callosum is the commissure of the neopallium.
Old cortex is joined by the old commissure. (Last's p. 594)
